Question: What are the control measures of Purple Blotch of Onion?

Answer: Purple blotch in onions, a fungal disease, can inflict significant yield and quality losses, especially under the high humidity (80–90%) and moderate temperatures (25–30 °C) typical of Sagar’s Rabi season . Managing this disease effectively requires a combination of cultural practices and timely fungicide application. Start with crop rotation for 2–3 years with non-host crops, maintain proper plant spacing, and use drip or furrow irrigation to reduce leaf wetness . Post-harvest, ensure thorough sanitation by removing and destroying infected residues. At the first signs of disease, spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 500g per acre or Chlorothalonil 75% WP at 800 g per acre, each mixed in 200 liters of water. For stronger and longer-lasting protection, use systemic fungicides like Propiconazole 25% EC or Tebuconazole 25% EC at 200 ml per acre, also in 200 liters of water. Repeat sprays every 10–15 days, depending on disease pressure and weather.

Question: How to control Wilt disease in Moong(Green gram)?

Answer: Moong is not suitable for Rabi season in Madhya Pradesh because the crop needs warm and humid weather, while the Rabi season is cool and dry; it grows best in Kharif with good rainfall and in Zaid (summer) with irrigation and higher temperature. Wilt disease in Moong(Green gram) is mainly caused by  Fusarium oxysporum. The disease can lead to significant yield losses, and once the pathogens are in the soil, they are very difficult to eradicate. Infected plant show sudden wilting, root may rot and plant growth stunted. To control this, an integrated disease management approach, combining cultural, biological, and chemical measures are recommended. Avoid continuous cropping of moong in the same field, practice crop rotation with sorghum or maize, remove and destroy all infected plant debris after harvest, and solarize soil using transparent polythene before sowing. Treat seed with Captan 50% WP @ 2g/kg seed or Carbendazim 50 WP @ 2g/kg or Thiram 75% WP @ 3g/kg or bioagent like Trichoderma viride/harzianum @ 4-6 g/kg  before sowing. Apply neem cake 80-100 kg per acre along with farm yard manure in soil during sowing, which can reduce wilt incidence.

Question: What is the procedure for making Nimboli ark (Neem Seed Kernel Extract)?

Answer: Nimboli Ark is a traditional, eco-friendly insecticide and growth booster prepared from neem seeds (nimboli) and widely used by farmers in Maharashtra for controlling sucking pests like aphids, jassids, thrips, whiteflies, and caterpillars in crops such as cotton, vegetables, pulses, and fruits. It works mainly because neem contains Azadirachtin, which acts as a feeding deterrent, growth regulator, and repellent. To prepare Nimboli ark, First Collect mature neem seeds (nimboli) from healthy neem trees. Remove the pulp if fresh fruits are used, and dry the seeds in shade for 2–3 days until the moisture is reduced. Then take 5 kg dried neem seeds and crush them coarsely using a grinder or mortar-pestle (do not make a fine powder, as this makes filtering difficult). Then soak the crushed seeds in 10 liters of clean water in an earthen, plastic, or wooden container (avoid metal) for 12 hours (overnight). Then the Next morning, knead and squeeze the soaked material well with your hands, and then filter it through a clean cotton cloth or fine mesh to remove solid particles. Add more water to make a final volume of 100 liters of neem extract. For better sticking to leaves, add 10–15 g of mild soap powder or 10 ml liquid soap while preparing the spray solution. Spray 5% Nimboli Ark: This means 5 liters of prepared neem seed extract in 100 liters of water, for small-scale preparation, on 500 ml extract in 10 liters of water. For thorough coverage of a field crop, spray 150-200 litres of the final solution per acre. Spray on both sides of the leaves to ensure full coverage. Start spraying at the early stage of pest appearance; do not wait for severe infestation. Use during cooler hours of the day (morning or evening) to increase effectiveness. Repeat spray every 7–10 days if pests persist. It can be used in all seasons, but in Kharif and Rabi crops in Maharashtra, it is particularly useful during high humidity and pest-prone periods. It is very Safe for beneficial insects like honeybees and natural enemies. No chemical residues suitable for organic farming, reduces pest population gradually and prevents resistance buildup, has a low cost, and can be prepared on-farm.

Question: Which flax (alsi) varieties are best for cultivation in Muktsar, Punjab?

Answer: For growing Alsi (flax) in Punjab, the best sowing time is mid-October to mid-November, because the crop likes cool weather and matures well before peak winter. Use 10 - 15 kg seed per acre for a good stand. PAU-approved varieties are NIA-7 (sturdy, disease tolerant, high yield), T-397 (early maturing with good fiber), and Shalimar Flax-2 (high oil content, resistant to major diseases, LC 2063 (this variety is for irrigated areas, resistant to powdery mildew. Its average yield is 4-5 qtl per acre), LC 2023 (This variety is suggested in irrigated as well as rain fed areas, seed contain 37.5% oil and yield 4.5 q/acre, resistent to downey mildew), Lc 54 (White flowers, brown seeds; lodging-resistant; adapted to multiple northern states), These varieties suit Punjab’s soil and climate, and can give you around 12–15 quintals yield per acre. Treat seed with Thiram @ 2 g/kg or Trichoderma viride 5 gram per kg of seeds to protect from seed and soil-borne diseases. For fertilizers, apply 25 - 30 kg Nitrogen (half at sowing, half at early growth after 35 days of sowing), 16 kg Phosphorus at sowing, and 20 kg Potash (if soil test shows deficiency, if needed only). Keep row spacing at 23 cm and plant spacing at 7 - 10 cm for proper growth. The crop gets ready in 110–120 days, harvest when capsules turn brown and straw dries, but cut carefully to avoid seed loss. Rotate with wheat or mustard to keep soil healthy and reduce disease. By following these steps, you will get good oil quality, higher yield, and better profit from your Alsi crop in Punjab.

Question: How can I prepare fertilizer grade 23:23:00 at my farm using DAP and Urea?

Answer: You can make fertilizer grade 23:23:00 in your farm using DAP and Urea. First, you need to understand the content of DAP and Urea, which is that DAP contains 18% Nitrogen and 46% Phosphorus, which makes its grade 18:46:00, and Urea contains only 46% Nitrogen, which makes its grade 46:00:00. To create 100 kg of 23:23:00, which contains 23% Nitrogen 23% Phosphorus, and some nitrogen. You need to mix the 50kg DAP, which gives you 23% phosphorus, and 30.5 kg Urea, which gives the remaining Nitrogen to complete the 23% and 15 kg filler material (sand, soil, dolomite powder). Question: How to control red cotton bug in okra?

Answer: Okra is a warm-season crop and is cultivated throughout the year in Madhya Pradesh, with the following main sowing periods: Kharif (Monsoon) season: The main sowing season is from June to July. Summer season: Sowing is typically done in February to March. The Red Cotton Bug (Dysdercus cingulatus), commonly name the "red fly" among farmers, is a common pest of Okra (Bhindi) in Madhya Pradesh. Both the nymphs and adult Red Cotton Bugs are sap-sucking pests. They feed on the tender shoots, leaves, and particularly the developing pods. Feeding on the pods causes the seeds to shrivel and the pods to become stunted and deformed. The bugs excrete a sticky, reddish fluid that stains the pods, making them unattractive and unmarketable. This also affects the quality of the seeds if the crop is grown for seed production. Their feeding can create entry points for fungal and bacterial pathogens, further damaging the pods. An integrated pest management (IPM) approach is the most effective way to control the Red Cotton Bug (Red fly). Remove and destroy crop residue from previous seasons, as it can harbor pests and their eggs. Keep the field and surrounding areas free of weeds, which can act as alternative host plants. In the early stages of infestation, you can manually collect and destroy the bugs, especially from the tender pods and leaves.  In the early stages of infestation, you can manually collect and destroy the bugs, especially from the tender pods and leaves. Sowing at the recommended time can help the crop escape the peak pest population. If the infestation is severe and other methods are not sufficient, chemical control can be used, such as Lambda-cyhalothrin 5% EC @ 200 ml per acre (PHI-5 days), Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 40-60 grams per acre (PHI-3 days), Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 60-80 ml per acre (PHI- 3 days). Always use a high volume of water, typically 200 liters per acre, to ensure complete coverage of the plants, especially the underside of the leaves and the developing pods where the bugs congregate. To prevent the development of insecticide resistance, it is crucial to rotate different classes of chemicals. Do not use the same chemical repeatedly. Always wear personal protective equipment (PPE) like gloves, a mask, and goggles while handling and spraying chemicals.

Question: How to control weeds in Barley?

Answer: Common broadleaf weeds in barley, such as Bathua, Senji (Methi), and Hirankhuri, can be effectively controlled by spraying Metsulfuron-methyl at 8 g per acre around 25–30 days after sowing. For grass weeds like Madusi (Phalaris minor) and Wild oat, post-emergence herbicides such as Axial (Pinoxaden 5% EC) at 400 ml per acre or Atlantis (Mesosulfuron-methyl 3% + Iodosulfuron-methyl sodium 0.6% WG) at 160 g per acre are recommended. For early weed control, apply a pre-emergence herbicide like Stomp (Pendimethalin 30% EC) at 1.3 liters per acre either just before or within two days of sowing. It is important to rotate herbicides with different modes of action each year. Always remember that when applying Atlantis, always add a recommended surfactant (such as a non-ionic surfactant or company-approved adjuvant) to ensure effective absorption and control.

Question: How to control Downy Mildew in Muskmelon?

Answer: Downy mildew in muskmelon causes yellow angular spots on the upper leaf surface, grayish-purple fungal growth on the lower leaf surface, and reduced fruit quality and yield. To control downy mildew in muskmelon, an integrated disease management approach combining cultural, mechanical, and chemical measures is recommended. Avoid planting muskmelons or other cucurbits (cucumber, bottle gourd) in the same field year after year and rotate with legumes or vegetables. Grow muskmelon in well-drained soil with good sunlight exposure, and avoid overhead irrigation to reduce leaf wetness. Spray protective fungicides, i.e., Mancozeb 75 WP @ 600-800 grams per acre mixed in 200 litres of water, before the disease appears or at the first sign of infection at 7-12 day intervals, or spray a combination of Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 500-800 grams per acre mixed with 200-250 litres of water and spray at every 7-10 day interval depending on disease pressure. The PHI (pre-harvest interval) period for mancozeb and metalaxyl + mancozeb is 7 days.

Question: Information regarding the plantation of Jasmine?

Answer: Jasmine thrives in well-drained, rich loamy soils with a pH ranging from 6.5 to 7.5. It prefers a mild, tropical climate with warm summers, mild winters, moderate rainfall, and sunny days. Jasmine is propagated through cuttings, layering, suckers, grafting, budding, and tissue culture. Cuttings: Semi-hardwood cuttings (15–20 cm long) are a popular method. Layering: This involves burying a mature shoot in the soil, which then develops roots. The cultivation of jasmine is quite popular, primarily for its fragrant flowers used in garlands, religious offerings, and the extraction of essential oils for perfumes and cosmetics. The best time for planting in North India (including Punjab) is July–August or January–February. Flowers are harvested as unopened buds by hand-picking in the early morning. Jasmine begins to produce commercial yields from the third year onwards and can continue for 10–15 years. The high-yielding jasmine variety officially recommended by PAU is Punjab Motiya. Spacing: 1.5 m × 1.5 m (about 1,799 plants per acre). Pruning: Mid-January is generally recommended for pruning in this region. Pruning during this time helps promote a maximum number of branches and a higher flower yield.

Question: How to control fruit flies in a bottle gourd?

Answer: Fruit fly is a serious pest in the bottle guard, causing fruits to rot from the inside, drop early and un unfit for market sale. To control fruit flies in a bottle guard, use 8-12 pheromone traps per acre to attract and lure the fruit flies. Use bait sprays like Hydrolysed protein bait spray @10-20 litres per acre, or you can mix 20 kg jaggery + Malathion 50 EC @ 10-30 ml mix in 20 litres of water and use as a bait spray for 1 acre. Give spray spinosad 45% SC @ 0.4 ml/litre of water or Lambda cyhalothrin 5% EC @ 1.5-2 ml/litre of water. Always rotate sprays so pests can not develop resistance to only one content. Collect and bury the fallen or infected fruits, and cover young fruits with polybags.

Question: What is the use of axial in wheat crop?

Answer: Axial is a post emergence herbicide widely used in Punjab for controlling Phalaris Minor(gulli danda) weed in Wheat cultivation. It contains Pinoxaden 5.1%. The recommended dose of Axial is 400 ml per acre in 200-250 litres of water and best time of spray when phalaris minor weed is at 3-5 leaf stage, usually around 30-35 days after sowing. Axial should be sprayed using a knapsack sprayer or tractor-mounted sprayer with a flat fan or floodjet nozzle to ensure thorough coverage of the weeds.

Question: When should I destroy the paddy plant?

Answer: Paddy stubble and leftover plants should be destroyed promptly after harvest completion. In some regions, this destruction should ideally be completed before November 15 each year. Timely destruction prevents various insect pests from surviving and multiplying in the crop residues.
The yellow stem borer and pink stem borer larvae remain protected inside leftover stems. These borers cause dead hearts in young plants and white ear heads in mature crops during subsequent seasons. Leaf folder larvae also survive in crop residues, hiding within folded leaves where they damage plants by scraping green tissue.
Planthoppers, including the brown plant hopper and white-backed plant hopper, take shelter in stubble. These sap-sucking insects not only weaken plants but also transmit dangerous viral diseases. Heavy infestations lead to hopper burn symptoms. Armyworm caterpillars feed on remaining plant material before moving to new crops, capable of rapid defoliation. Rice hispa beetles and their grubs survive in stubble, causing characteristic white streaks on leaves of new plants. You can do deep ploughing to 10-12 inch depth, which completely buries stubble and associated pests. Chemical options involve spraying glyphosate at 10 ml/liter or paraquat at 5 ml/liter on standing stubble within one week post-harvest. These applications kill pests and prevent regrowth.

Question: For Finger millet, which method is better: dibbling or transplanting?

Answer: Dibbling is better than transplanting for finger millet. Dibbling saves labour, needs less water, conserves moisture for a long time, is easier for hilly and rainfed areas, and is cost-effective. Growing plants by direct dibbling after the first good rain gives better crop stand and root development. Transplanting is more labour-intensive and needs a nursery, which is not practical for many farmers in the region. Use improved, region-tested varieties like VM 4 (VL Mandua 4) or Narendra Mandua 4, which are promoted by ICAR-RCNEH, Basar and the Arunachal Pradesh Krishi Vigyan Kendras for local rainfed conditions. They are known for good yield potential and adaptability to the Northeast’s climate. The recommended seed rate of 6-7 kg per acre and spacing of 25 × 10 cm are correct for this method. After sowing, to control weeds, apply Pendimethalin 30% EC @ 1 litre per acre as pre-emergence within 3 days of sowing. Mix in 200 - 250 litres of water and spray evenly for full coverage. If a second flush of weeds appears, do one hand weeding at 20–25 days after sowing. Before sowing, apply 2 quintals of compost and 5 kg Trichoderma per acre to improve soil health and manage soil-borne diseases. This is a highly recommended and sustainable approach. Keep the field clean for the first 40 days. This simple method gives strong root growth, better tillering, and good yield under Arunachal’s local conditions.

Question: Information regarding Cineraria Plants

Answer: Cineraria is a popular ornamental flowering plant grown for its bright, daisy-like blooms in various colors. There are some popular varieties include Grandiflora, Senetti, and Cruentus Hybrids, which offer vibrant flowers. The recommended seed rate for cineraria is 100-150 grams per acre for commercial cultivation. For home gardening, sowing 2-3 seeds per small pot is sufficient before transplanting. The ideal sowing time in your region is September to October for winter flowering displays. For pot cultivation, you can produce 50,000-60,000 marketable plants/acre. Seeds typically germinate in 10-15 days under optimal conditions. Transplanting should be done 4-5 weeks after sowing for best results. Flowering begins 12-14 weeks after sowing and continues for 6-8 weeks. Peak flowering occurs from December to February in Punjab's climate. Cineraria prefers well-drained, fertile soil. Pests like aphids can be controlled using neem-based organic sprays. You should apply 5-6 tons of FYM per acre as basal fertilizer.Supplemental NPK fertilizer at 20:20:20 kg per acre enhances plant growth. Proper post-harvest handling maintains flower quality for a longer shelf life.

Question: How to control burn in Maize?

Answer: If burn or toxicity appears in maize, then first remember everything must be done in balance. Apply fertilizers based on soil test, because excess nitrogen or potash will burn the leaves. Use farmyard manure or compost to keep the soil healthy and reduce stress on plants. Irrigation must be given timely, neither too much nor too little—because both drought and waterlogging increase burn. Keep the field clean of weeds, as they take away water and nutrients. When using herbicides like Atrazine or Tembotrione, always maintain the right dose, otherwise it will harm the maize itself. Proper pest control keeps plants strong and reduces the chance of burn. Crop rotation is also very important, changing crops keeps soil healthy and reduces disease pressure. After harvest, always remove leftover crop residues, otherwise soil-borne problems will increase. Use tolerant maize varieties whenever possible, and always sow treated seeds so seedlings grow strong. If needed, foliar sprays like Mancozeb or Metalaxyl can be used to control fungal problems, but only at the recommended dose, because overdose will worsen the burn. Maintain proper spraying intervals and follow safety rules. By managing these small but important practices, maize plants will stay healthy, burn will be less, and yield will be better.

Question: When is the sowing time of Turmeric?

Answer: Turmeric being a water dependent long duration crop it is advisable to use some irrigation methods along with selection of well drained soil. 
The ideal timing of sowing Turmeric from April to May(Kharif season crop) .It should preferably coincide with the summer rains. If sowing is done during summer irrigation is necessary. 
The seed rate of turmeric is around 8-10 quintals for an acre. 
The most famous variety to choose is IISR Pragati which is a short duration variety with a potential yield of 21 tons for an acre.
Pre-sprouting of selected rhizomes should be ensure sprout viability. It is achieved by keeping the rhizomes in warm humid place mostly in moist sand, saw dust or coconut husk. New green shoots will emerge within 7-15 days.

Question: What is the yellow revolution?

Answer: The Yellow Revolution in India refers to the national drive to increase oilseed production, particularly soybean, sunflower, mustard, groundnut, and safflower. It began in 1986–1990 under the Technology Mission on Oilseeds (TMO), launched to reduce India’s dependence on edible oil imports, Adopt modern techniques for oil seeds crop, enhance farmer income,. Maharashtra played a pivotal part because large areas, especially Vidarbha and Marathwada, are ideally suited for oilseed crops. Soybean emerged as a dominant Kharif crop in these regions, while safflower and sunflower became key Rabi season crops. Using strategies like high-yielding seed varieties, improved irrigation methods, timely pest and disease control, and balanced fertilizer use. Government support through seed subsidies, irrigation incentives, MSP for oilseeds, and farmer training programs. Before the mission, India’s oilseed production was about 11–12 million metric tonnes (MMT). By the mid-1990s, the Yellow Revolution had doubled production to around 25 MMT. This breakthrough laid the foundation for continued growth, reaching 40–60 MMT in later decades through sustained research, better technology, and supportive policies. Maharashtra earned the title of India’s soybean capital during this period. Bodies like the Maharashtra State Oilseeds Growers’ Federation (MSOILFED) continue to promote oilseed farming through seed distribution, market linkages, and processing support. Future Goals of the yellow revolutions are doubling oilseed yield by 2030 through advanced breeding and adoption of GM crops (e.g., herbicide-tolerant mustard), solar-powered oil mills to cut processing costs and improve profitability

Question: What are the varieties of Tomato in Jabalpur?

Answer: For a farmer in Madhya Pradesh, the best strategy is to select a variety based on their specific needs and the time of year they are planting.                                                                                                                For the rabi season season the recommended tomato varieties are: Pusa Ruby(mature within 60-65 days, use for table and processing purpose and yield 130 quintals per acre), Pusa early dwarf(matures within 75-80 days after transplanting, suitable for both table and processing, yield 140 quintals per acre), and Kashi Chyan(matures in 140 days, resistant to ToYLCVD, yield 280 quintals per acre).                                                                                                                                                           Varieties recommended for kharif season: Kashi Vishesh(tolerance to the challenges of the rainy season, matures within 73 days after planting), Arka Rakshak(offers triple resistance to Bacterial Wilt, Tomato Leaf Curl Virus (ToLCV), and Early Blight disease), Arka Anupam( tolerance to Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus) and Kashi Chyan(it is also suitable for humid condition).                                    Varieties suitable for Zaid season are: Pusa Shakti(heat tolerant, yield 140 quintals per acre), Vaishali and Pusa Hybrid 1.

Question: How to control Caterpillar attack in Gram?

Answer: The pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera) is the most destructive pest of gram, causing 20–30% yield loss, and in severe cases up to 70–80%. The caterpillars hatch from round, pearl-like eggs and initially scrape tender leaves before boring into pods and feeding on the grains inside. For management, an integrated approach is essential.

Install sex pheromone traps (when 4–5 moths/trap/night are caught, control measures should start), adopt agronomic practices like deep summer plowing, timely sowing, and intercropping with mustard, coriander, or linseed, and plant yellow marigold as a trap crop to divert egg-laying.

Biological control includes spraying Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus (NPV) @ 250 larval equivalents per acre, conserving insectivorous birds by erecting T-shaped perches, and encouraging parasitoids by growing pollen-rich crops. Neem seed (Nimboli) extract prepared from 5 kg seed in 10 litres water plus 200 g washing powder, diluted in 100 litres water, can be sprayed per acre.

When necessary, chemical options include Spinosad 45 SC @ 75 ml or Chlorantraniliprole 18.5 SC @ 60 ml/acre in 200 litres of water. The pre-harvest interval needed is 21 days for Spinosad and 18 days for Chlorantraniliprole.

Question: Information regarding the management of the crop from frost

Answer: Frost can be a significant threat to crops in Guna, Madhya Pradesh, especially during the winter months of December and January. Effective management involves both passive and active techniques to mitigate damage. Avoid planting frost-sensitive crops in low-lying areas where cold air can accumulate. Choose crop varieties that are more tolerant to frost or have a later flowering/bud break period. Keep the soil moist through irrigation before a frost event. Wet soil stores and transfers heat better than dry soil. This can help release heat during the night, slightly raising the air temperature near the ground. Avoid applying nitrogen fertilizer in late summer or early autumn, as this can promote vegetative growth that is more susceptible to frost. Ensure that plants are not deficient in potassium, which can help them maintain cell water content and potentially improve their tolerance to frost. Using row covers, frost blankets, or plastic sheeting can help trap heat and create a microclimate around the plants. Applying mulch (e.g., straw, leaves) at the base of plants can insulate the soil and roots, reducing temperature fluctuations. Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY): This is a key crop insurance scheme that provides comprehensive coverage against crop losses due to natural calamities, including frost. Farmers in notified areas cultivating notified crops can avail themselves of this scheme.

Question: Information regarding the seed treatment of green Gram

Answer: Seed treatment in green gram before sowing is very important because it protects the seed from fungus and soil brone diases along with helps the crop to grow fast and healthy. First do fungicide treatment – mix Carbendazim 1 g + Captan 2 g per kg seed (total 3 gram per kg of seed) (but. applied onlu under exapert guidance as it have under some restriction). This protects the seed from rot, damping off, and soil fungi. After that, do biofertilizer treatment – apply Rhizobium culture 5 gram per kg of seed. Rhizobium fixes nitrogen from the air into the soil, which saves fertilizer cost and increases yield. The method is simple – first coat the seeds well with fungicide powder in a dry container, then dry for 15–20 minutes. After that, prepare a solution of jaggery or sugar water, mix Rhizobium in it, and coat the seeds so the culture sticks properly. Sowing should be done immediately after treatment; do not store treated seeds for long. As carbendazim have restriction in that case you may use Thiram 2.5 g/kg or Captan 3 g/kg alone, but Rhizobium treatment is a must in pulses for nitrogen fixation. If you follow this step, seeds will be safe, crop will be strong, nitrogen will be available naturally, and production will definitely increase.

Question: what is samba variety in rice?

Answer: For the Zaid season (March to June) in Thiruvallur, Tamil Nadu, it is crucial to choose extra-short duration rice varieties that can mature within the limited window of this hot and dry season. Kar/Kuruvai varieties are the right choice for Zaid, as they are bred to withstand the heat and shorter growing period. Question: What is the msp of mint crop?

Answer: The MSP policy in India has only 23 commodities including staples like cereals, pulses, oilseeds, and commercial crops such as cotton and jute—but mint is not there Because mint isn’t included in the MSP list and isn’t a widely procured crop, there is no government-set MSP for mint.That said, horticultural or perishable crops like mint may sometimes receive temporary support through schemes like the Market Intervention Scheme (MIS), but such measures are case-specific and limited.

Question: How to control early blight in Tomato?

Answer: Early blight in tomato is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani and is a major disease that affects leaves, stems, and sometimes fruits, leading to yield loss. symptoms- Leaf spots: Brown to black concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves, Leaf drying: Starts from lower leaves and progresses upward, Stem lesions: Dark, elongated spots on stems, Fruit infection: Dark sunken spots near the stalk end. To control early blight in tomato should follow (IDM) Cultural practices- Use disease-free seeds and resistant varieties, Remove and destroy infected plant debris, mulching to prevent soil splash on leaves. Treat the seeds Carbendazim 50 WP @ 2 g/kg seed or Thiram @ 2.5 g/kg seed. Biological control-Apply Trichoderma harzianum or viride @ 5 g/kg seed, Drench soil with Trichoderma formulation mixed in FYM at transplanting. Chemical control- Apply a protective fungicide such as Hexaconazole early in the season, alternate with curative options like Difenoconazole or the Azoxystrobin + Tebuconazole mix once disease symptoms begin. Spray Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP: 300 grams per acre, PHI- 7 days or Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC: 200 ml per acre, 3 days, Mix the recommended dose with 200-300 liters of water for a thorough foliar spray.

Question: What are the improved varieties of Garlic?

Answer: Garlic is a high-value crop, and choosing the right variety can increase your profit. Agrifound White (G-41) is a popular choice, giving around 50–55 quintals per acre, with compact white bulbs that store well. Yamuna Safed (G-282) performs well too, offering a yield of about 60-70 quintals per acre, with uniform large bulbs and good market price. For those aiming for extra-large cloves and even better yield, G-323 is a strong option, giving 65-70 quintals per acre. These varieties not only fetch better rates but also reduce storage losses.

Question: Information regarding the HRC 127 and HRC 47 varieties

Answer: Cotton varieties like HRC 127 and HRC 47 are not officially recommended for cultivation in Punjab. Farmers must plant only the current year’s PAU-certified Bt cotton hybrids (87 approved hybrids in 2025), which are resistant to Pink Bollworm and other pests. Select desi varieties like LD 949, LD 1019, and FDK 124 are also promoted for diversification. Effective pest management practices are also critical, such as removing cotton stalks and residues after harvest, controlling weeds to reduce whitefly populations, and maintaining hygiene in ginning facilities to prevent pest spread. Farmers should always source seeds from official, certified suppliers and avoid outdated varieties to maximize yield and minimize pest damage.

Question: How to control Yellow Mosaic in Papaya?

Answer: Yellow mosaic in papaya is a devastating viral disease, transmitted by aphid and whitefly. Symptoms including yellowing of leaves in a mosaic pattern, leaf curling, stunted growth, and reduced fruit size. There is no direct cure for viral infection once the plant is infected. Therefore, it is necessary to control whiteflies and aphids to prevent spreading of the disease. As soon as you see the first symptoms of yellow mosaic, immediately uproot and destroy the entire plants. Plant virus free seedlings from a reliable nursery. Keep the field and and surrounding areas free of weeds, maintain proper plant spacing, Apply silver or white plastic mulch can repel whiteflies, especially during the early stages of plant growth and spray sturdy plants with a strong jet of water which can deter whiteflies and aphids. Encourage natural predators such as ladybird beetles and lacewings. For organic control, prepare a tobacco decoction by boiling 1 kg of tobacco in 10 litres of water for 30 minutes, then dilute the mixture to 30 litres and add 100 g of insecticidal soap, which can reduce whiteflies and aphids population. In case of severe infestation or if you see mosaic symptoms such as yellowing or mosaic patterns on new leaves, spray Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.3-0.5 ml per litre of water or Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 0.3 gram per litre of water at 10-15 days interval.

Question: What is the trade name of Indoxacarb?

Answer: Indoxacarb was available in the market with trade names of Doxagan (indoxacarb 14.5%SC) from Adama ,K-Indox (indoxacarb 14.5%SC) from Katyayani organics ,King doxa(indoxacarb 14.5%SC) from Gharda chemicals. This chemical mainly used to control Borers and ,sucking pests.

Question: Which are the diseases in methi and how can I control it?

Answer: Fenugreek (Methi) is a strong plant, but sometimes it gets sick, especially when the soil is too wet. One common problem is Powdery Mildew. It looks like white powder on the leaves and stems and makes the plant weak. Another problem is Root Rot and Damping Off. These make young plants fall over and die. Downy Mildew shows yellow spots on the leaves and gray color underneath..For Powdery Mildew, foliar spray with Sulphur 80% WP at 2.5 g/litre of water with waiting period of 15 days or Carbendazim 50% WP at 1 g/litre with waiting period of10 days is recommended. For Downy Mildew, spraying Mancozeb 75% WP at 2.5 g/litre with waiting period of 7 days or Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (e.g., Ridomil Gold) at 2 g/litre with waiting period of 21 days is effective. For Root Rot and Damping Off, soil drenching with Carbendazim or Captan at 2 g/litre is useful, with a general waiting period of 15 days before harvest. Alongside chemical control, farmers should also follow cultural practices like using clean soil, avoiding excess watering, maintaining proper spacing, and removing infected plants. These steps ensure healthy growth and reduce the risk of disease in the fenugreek crop.

Question: How can I control blast disease in mustard crops in Bathinda, Punjab?

Answer: Cumin (Jeera) is a major spice crop, traditionally cultivated in Rajasthan and Gujarat. However, with the right practices, it can be a profitable crop for farmers in Punjab, including Sangrur. The key to successful cumin cultivation is managing the specific climatic requirements, as the crop is very sensitive to humidity and frost. The optimal sowing time for cumin in Sangrur is from mid-October to mid-November. Sowing should be done in a way that the crop's flowering period avoids the peak humidity that can occur with unseasonal winter rains, which have become a normal phenomenon in Punjab. The correct seed rate for cumin is 8-10 kg/acre for line sowing or 10-12 kg/acre for broadcasting. Treat the seeds with a fungicide like Carbendazim 50% WP @ 2-3 grams per kilogram of seed to prevent seed-borne diseases.

Question: There is  too much saline in my field how can I manage it?

Answer: In Punjab some fields have saline soil where too much salt in the top layer stops good germination, burns young roots, and cuts crop yield badly. As per PAU, the first step is always to do a soil test from an authorised lab to know the exact salt problem and calculate the right dose of amendment. For chemical control, apply Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) @ about 1.5 - 6 tones per acre or as per soil test report. Broadcast it evenly on a moist, well-prepared field, mix it into the top 10–15 cm soil, and give one good irrigation. Gypsum replaces harmful sodium salts with calcium and improves soil structure for many years. You can also use Phospho-gypsum of equal purity and dose. For biological control, grow salt-tolerant green manure crops like Dhaincha (Sesbania aculeata) or Sunhemp in summer, then plough them into the soil at flowering stage. This adds organic matter, improves drainage, and reduces salt effect naturally. For cultural control, you can use PAU‑recommended salt‑tolerant varieties like CSR‑30 (paddy), PR‑126 (early paddy), PBW‑869 (wheat), keep fields well‑levelled, give light but frequent irrigations, ensure drainage to flush salts, avoid stagnant water, and rotate with tolerant crops like berseem or mustard. Since these are soil amendments, PHI does not apply, and crops can be sown immediately after reclamation irrigation. This integrated method improves yield, keeps soil healthy, and gives lasting benefit.

Question: What is the seed rate of the Lentil crop?

Answer: Lentil in Haryana is grown as a Rabi season crop than Kharif crop due to its sensitivity to moisture.

Seed rate for small seeded lentil under both rainfed and irrigated condition is 15-18Kg/acre. For Bold seeded type under both rainfed and irrigated condition is 18-20Kg/acre. The sowing season is from Mid-October to Mid-November.

Question: What care should I take while preparing a nursery bed for vegetable crops?

Answer: The major crops grown on raised seedlings in nursery beds are vegetables like tomato, brinjal, cucumber, chilli, cabbage, capsicum, papaya, citrus, and paddy, especially in regions with heavy black soils. Because it improves drainage, helps in root development, and is easy for drip irrigation. Prepare raised beds about 15-20 cm high to prevent waterlogging. Width: 1m-1.2 m (for easy management), length: As per space. Treating raised beds before sowings is very important to ensure healthy soil, reduce pest and disease risks, and improve crop productivity.  To treat nursery beds, you can do First soil solarization 3-4 weeks before sowing, give organic treatment like FYM (2-3 tonnes/acre), Vermicompost  (4-5 tonnes/acre), Neem cake  (200-300 kg/acre) at the time of land preparation. You can also use mulch to prevent weeds and moisture retention, and to reduce soil-borne diseases.

Question: What are the recommended seed treatment practices in soybean?

Answer: Treat the seed with a mixture of  Thiram + Carboxin @ 2.5-3 g/kg seed, or Thiamethoxam 78WS @ 12 g/kg seed, or Trichoderma viride @ 4-5 g/kg seed.

Biofertilizers like Rhizobium (Bradyrhizobium japonicum) @ 5-10 g/kg seed and PSB (Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria) @ 5-10 g/kg seed should also be applied a few hours before sowing, while 2.5 kg PSB per acre may be mixed in the soil for better phosphorus availability.

Sowing should ideally be done between the last week of June and the first week of July, once there is 4–5 inches of rainfall. For less spreading varieties (JS 93-05, JS 95-60), maintain 40 cm row spacing, while for wide spreading ones (JS 335, NRC 7, JS 97-52), keep 45 cm spacing. The seed rate for an acre is 24–28 kg for small grain varieties and 32–36 kg for large grain varieties, targeting a population of 1.6–1.8 lakh plants per acre. In deep black soils and high rainfall areas, sowing is best done with Ridger Seeder Planter using furrow ridge method or Raised Bed Planter. It should avoid mixing chemical fertilizers directly with seeds during sowing.

Question: How to control Gall midge (GANGAI) in Paddy crop?

Answer: Gall midge in paddy can be managed well if we follow proper integrated practices from the start. After harvest, plough the ratoon crop deeply and remove grassy weeds or wild rice around the field because they act as host plants. Do not do staggered planting; finish sowing within 3 weeks, and prefer early planting with resistant varieties like Bhadrakali, Pavitra, Panchami, Indursamba, Vasundhara, Shaktiman, Divya, Suraksha, Rashmi, Karna Mahavir, Rajendradhan 202, Birsa Dhan 202 and others suitable for Madhya Pradesh. Apply nitrogen and potash in split doses, but avoid excess nitrogen as it increases pest attack. In nursery, clip the tips of seedlings before transplanting, remove and burn infested plants, and use coir rope dragging to dislodge pests. Also drain the crop for 5–7 days during sensitive stage to reduce larvae. For biological help, protect natural enemies like parasitoid wasp Platygaster oryzae, predatory mites, and spiders, release parasitized eggs per acre at egg stage, about 10 days after transplanting. For chemical protection, in nursery or early crop stage, you may use Carbosulfan 6% G 6.7 kg per acre in nursery. As an another option you may choose Carbosulfan 25% EC 320 to 400 ml per acre Mix this dose in 150 to 200 liters of water per acre for even spraying coverage. At at 20 days after transplanting apply Fipronil 0.3% GR 6.7 to 10 lbs per acre or as an alternatilvely also you can use  Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC at a dose of 40-50 ml/acre in 200 liters of water with 47 days of interval period. Alternatively, spray Thiamethoxam 25% WG at a dose of 40 grams/acre in 200 liters of water with 21 days of interval period. Another effective option is Imidacloprid 17.8% SL at a dose of 40-50 ml/acre in 200 liters of water with 40 days of interval period. For best results, apply the spray during the early morning or late evening hours. Avoid repeated use of the same chemical class to prevent the development of resistance in the pest population. Use pheromone and light traps (5 traps per acre) for monitoring pest, and spray only when pest population crosses economic threshold to check pest activity. Remember PHI (waiting period before harvest) for Carbosulfan and Fipronil is 60 days, and also mentioned others chemical, so plan spray accordingly. By following these combined steps gall midge problem will stay under control and you will get a healthy and profitable paddy crop.

Question: What are the recommended cultivation practices for Citronella and from where I can procure seedlings?

Answer: Citronella is a fragrant grass plant known for its mosquito-repelling oil. It grows well due to its humid climate and rainfall. Farmers should use high-yielding varieties like Mandakini, Manjusha, or Jor Lab C-5, which are suitable for hilly areas and give higher oil yield. Use rooted slips only (not seeds), about 12,000–14,000 slips per acre, and maintain proper spacing of 60 cm × 60 cm, as it ensures proper plant growth and good air flow. The best time for planting is April to June, before the peak monsoon, and select well-drained, light loamy soil with good organic content. Apply 4–5 tons of FYM per acre before planting, and a basal dose of 40 kg of Nitrogen, 20 kg of Phosphorus, and 20 kg of Potash per acre. After each harvest, you can apply 40 kg of Nitrogen per acre to boost regrowth. You can get quality planting materials from a trusted source like ICAR Basar, KVK Papum Pare, or KVK West Siang. If you are doing it naturally, then keep the field weed-free for 2 months, and practice manual 2-round weeding at 20 and 40 days after planting and give light mulching with rice husk or straw to suppress weeds, which is cost-effective and safe. For chemical control, apply Glyphosate 41% SL @ 800 ml per acre in 200 – 250 litres of water before planting (on moist soil only). Do not spray on or near the citronella slips, as it is a non-selective herbicide that can damage the crop and cause phytotoxicity. Use 2% salt solution spray after planting for soft weeds. Citronella has low pest risk, but for leaf spot disease, spray Copper oxychloride 50% WP @ 600 grams per acre mixed in 200 liters of water and ensure sprayed evenly over the crop, and for insect safety, use Neem-based pesticide (Azadirachtin 1500 ppm) @ 500 ml per acre also mixed in 200 liters of water. First harvest starts after 4 months, then every 2.5–3 months, 4–5 cuttings per year are possible. Oil should be distilled within 24 hours for better quality. Use a knapsack or power sprayer, and spray in the morning or late afternoon when the temperature is cooler for best results. Always wear protective gear while spraying.

Question: Why are young garlic plants drying, and how can I prevent damping-off disease ?

Answer: One of the reasons for drying of young garlic plants can be a disease called damping-off, which is caused by soil-borne fungi like Pythium, Rhizoctonia, or Fusarium. In this disease, seedlings turn pale, their growth becomes stunted, and the stem portion near the soil line starts to soften, rot, and collapse. Often, the plants fall over and dry up in patches. The problem is more severe in waterlogged or poorly drained soils, and in fields where garlic or onion has been grown repeatedly. To prevent and control damping-off, always use healthy, disease-free cloves for planting and avoid sowing in infected soil. Before planting, treat cloves with thiram 75 WP (3 g per litre of water) and shade dry before sowing. If the symptoms appear on standing crop do drenching near the root zone using Copper Oxychloride 50 WP ( 3 gm per litre of water or 600 gm per acre) or Metalaxyl-M 4 + Mancozeb 64 WP (2.5 gm per litre of water) . Ensure proper field drainage and avoid over-irrigation. Crop rotation with non-host crops for at least 3 years also helps in reducing disease buildup. Timely care and field hygiene will protect your garlic crop and improve yield quality.

Question: What is the growing period of arbi in Ludhiana region?

Answer: In Punjab, the recommended growing period for arum (arbi) is highly dependent on the crop season. You can sow arbi during the first fortnight of February for the summer season, or in June to July for the rainy season crop. The crop requires about 160 to 180 days, approximately five to six months to reach maturity, depending on the specific variety and cultivation practices used. For the summer crop sown in February, harvesting generally takes place around July or August, while arbi planted in the rainy season is harvested in November or December. Optimal growth necessitates a warm climate, regular irrigation, and well-drained, organic-rich sandy loam soil, which helps prevent tuber rot and ensures healthy corm development throughout the growing period.

Question: What is KCC & its advantages to the farmers?

Answer: The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme in Madhya Pradesh is a central government scheme designed to provide timely and adequate credit support to farmers for their agricultural and allied activities. It is available to all types of farmers, including owner farmers, tenant farmers, Self Help Groups (SHGs), and Joint Liability Groups (JLGs). Farmers can use the loan amount for purchasing seeds, fertilizers, pesticides, irrigation, machinery, dairy, poultry, fisheries, goatery, and even limited household needs. The loan limit is decided based on landholding, cropping pattern, and scale of finance fixed by the District Level Technical Committee (DLTC). Loan amounts start from around ₹10,000 to ₹50,000 for small and marginal farmers and go up to ₹3–5 lakhs or more depending on requirements. The normal interest rate is 7% per annum, but farmers who repay on time may get a 3% interest subvention, so the effective interest rate becomes only 4%. The repayment period is one year for short-term crop loans and 3–5 years for term loans like tractors, pump sets, or dairy units. For loans up to ₹1.6 lakh, generally no collateral is required, while higher loans may need land documents as security. Farmers can apply for KCC in any nationalized bank, cooperative bank, or regional rural bank in Madhya Pradesh, such as SBI, PNB, Central Bank of India, MP Gramin Bank, or District Cooperative Bank, by filling the KCC application form. The documents required are an Aadhaar card, Voter ID or PAN card, land records (Khasra/Khatauni) or lease agreement in the case of tenants, passport-size photographs, and bank account details.

Question: How to cultivate Rubber in Arunachala Pradesh?

Answer: Rubber cultivation is possible in the Doimukh area of Arunachal Pradesh due to suitable rainfall and climate. Farmers should first select high-yielding varieties like RRII 105, RRII 430, RRIM 600 or PB 260, which are in good demand and suitable for hilly Northeast regions and are recommended by the Rubber Board. These varieties give good latex yield and are disease-tolerant. To get healthy and certified planting material, farmers can contact the Rubber Board Field Office at Naharlagun and approach registered nurseries under the Rubber Board or ICAR centres that supply certified planting materials. It is always better to use budded stumps or polybag plants of 6–8 months age for good survival and growth. Before planting, clear the land, do proper pit digging (60cm x 60cm x 60cm), and apply 5 kg compost and 50 gram single super phosphate (SSP) per pit. Maintain spacing of 3m x 7m which allows about 220 trees per acre for better growth and tapping access. After planting, mulch the base to retain moisture and control weeds. For weed control, apply pendimethalin 30% EC @ 1 litre per acre 200–240 litres of water, as a pre-emergence spray immediately after planting, which is safer and suitable for upland plantations. Use flat fan nozzle for uniform spray. Rubber trees require 6–7 years of growth before they are ready for tapping. Tapping begins when the tree reaches a girth of 50 cm at 120 cm height. Tapping should be done by using a sharp tapping knife to make a thin, half-spiral cut on the bark early in the morning. This technique allows latex to flow without harming the tree. Tapping should be done on alternate days or following a proper schedule, which helps in getting better and longer-lasting yields. Ethrel (ethephon) should only be used at 1.5% concentration after the third tapping season once in 30–45 days,  to avoid bark damage  — do not overuse. To earn a good price, farmers should collect latex in clean cups, use formic acid (150 ml per 10 litres latex) for coagulation, and avoid adding water or impurities. The rubber sheets must be well-washed, smoked, and dried properly. Selling through registered cooperatives or Rubber Producers’ Societies (RPS) ensures better market access and fair prices. Apply NPK 12:6:6 @ 12 kg per tree per year in 2–3 splits. Use Trichoderma during monsoon to protect roots. You can also grow pineapple or ginger between rows in early years for extra income. Register your plantation with Rubber Board to get subsidy, training, and support. With proper care, one acre can yield 300–500 kg of dry rubber annually from the 8th year onwards. Farmers are advised to start small, take expert guidance, and maintain the plantation properly. Rubber offers long-term income and growing market demand in Arunachal, making it a promising option for farmers in this region.

Question: How can I control Milk fever in Buffalo?

Answer: Milk fever is a metabolic disorder caused by low blood calcium levels, typically occurring around calving in high-yielding buffaloes. Early symptoms include restlessness, muscle tremors, stiffness while walking, and reduced appetite. Advanced symptoms include the animal being unable to stand, its head turned to the side in an S-shape, cold ears and body, lethargy, and coma. Immediate veterinary treatment is essential as this is a medical emergency. The standard treatment is a slow intravenous injection of Calcium Borogluconate administered by a veterinarian. A typical dosage is 200-300 ml of a 20-25% solution given slowly to avoid heart complications. Supportive care includes keeping the animal warm and comfortable during recovery. Do not give oral fluids or medicine to a downed animal due to the risk of choking. Prevention focuses on dietary management during the dry period. Feed a low calcium diet for 2-3 weeks before calving to activate the animal's calcium regulation. Avoid lush legume fodder like berseem which is high in potassium and can trigger milk fever. Veterinarians may recommend anionic salts to acidify the blood and help mobilize calcium. Give oral calcium boluses immediately after calving and again 12 hours later as a preventive measure. Avoid over- fattening animals during the dry period and provide a clean, non-slippery calving area. A veterinarian is essential for correct diagnosis, safe treatment, and designing a preventive plan.

Question: What is the process of Rearing chicks?

Answer: Chicken rearing in Tamil Nadu is a simple and sure income work if we follow right steps, broilers like Cobb 500, Vencobb and Ross 308 grow fast and reach near 2 kg weight in just 6–7 weeks, while layers like White Leghorn and Rhode Island Red lay around 250–280 eggs in a year, so first make clean shed with good airflow and dry litter using rice husk or sawdust, keep chicks warm at 32–35°C in starting and slowly reduce to 24°C when they grow, always give clean drinking water and proper feed with 22–24% protein for broilers and 16–18% for layers, layers also need 14–16 hours of light daily to maintain egg laying, keep shed neat, separate sick birds, disinfect well, and use probiotics for good digestion, medicines should be given only with doctor advice and remember withdrawal time before sale, vaccination against New Castle and Marek’s disease must be done in time, feed cost is big so save by giving right feed at right time, and if you use poultry droppings in farm do soil and water testing to avoid damage, always buy chicks from government hatcheries or TNAU recommended suppliers, if you do all these simple things, birds will be healthy, grow well and surely give you good money.

Question: How To Control Tela in Potato?

Answer: Jassids damage potato crops by sucking sap from the leaves, ans shows leaf curling, yellowing, and scorching along the margins, which can reduce photosynthesis and ultimately yield. To control them chemically, spray Confidor (Imidacloprid 17.8 SL) at 50-60 ml/acre, Actara (Thiamethoxam 25 WG) at 50 g/acre, or Pride (Acetamiprid 20 SP) at 50 g/acre. Ensure proper rotation of insecticides to delay resistance buildup. Importantly, waiting period must be 7–10 days before last spray to to avoid chemical residues in the tubers. Adopt cultural practices such as early planting to escape peak pest pressure, maintaining optimal plant spacing to improve airflow, and removing weeds and crop residues.

Question: What is khumba farming (mushroom cultivation)?

Answer: In Punjab, Khumba farming (mushroom cultivation) is becoming popular because it gives high returns in a short time and needs only a small space. The most common type grown here is white button mushroom (Agaricus bisporus), but farmers also grow oyster mushroom (Pleurotus species) and paddy straw mushroom (Volvariella species). For white button mushroom, the best season in Punjab is October to March, when the temperature is 14–22 °C. It is usually grown in a controlled room or shed using pasteurised compost prepared from wheat straw, poultry manure, and gypsum. For oyster mushroom, which grows well at 20–30 °C, farmers can use simple rooms and polybags filled with pasteurised straw. Use good quality spawn from reliable sources like Punjab Agricultural University (PAU), Ludhiana. For button mushrooms, the standard metric is the yield per quintal (100 kg) of ready compost. PAU and KVKs provide training in khumba farming, covering compost preparation, spawn running, harvesting, and marketing.

Question: How to increase growth of Guava Tree?

Answer: To promote vigorous growth in guava trees, young trees (1–3 years old) benefit significantly from an annual dose of around 10–15 kg of well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM) per tree, supplemented with balanced inorganic nutrients of approximately 50–100 g nitrogen , 25–50 g phosphorus , and 50–75 g potassium ,DAP 55–110 g, Urea 90–175 g and MOP 85–125 g) divided over 3–4 applications during the growing season. For mature trees (4+ years), raise the nutritional level to 20–25 kg FYM and apply 200–300 g N, 100–150 g P, and 200–250 g K (DAP 220–325 g, Urea 350–525 g, and MOP 335–420 g.) per tree annually, timed at critical stages: before flowering (Feb–Mar), post-fruit set (May–June), and post-harvest. Additionally, structured pruning—such as maintaining a low-headed open or modified leader system and thinning overcrowded branches—encourages a sturdy canopy structure, improves light penetration, and supports sustained growth and fruiting.

Question: How to control larvae in Gram (Chick Pea)?

Answer: Chickpea (Gram) is primarily a Rabi season crop. Gram Pod Borer Symptoms:
Grown-up larvae feed on buds, flowers, and pods. Developing and partly matured seeds are completely eaten by the larvae. While feeding, the head of the larva is inserted into the pod, and the rest of the body remains outside. A single larva may destroy 30–40 pods before it reaches maturity. To control Gram Pod Borer, follow Integrated Pest Management (IPM): Cultural Measures: Sow three rows of sorghum or maize as a border crop. Mechanical Control: Install pheromone traps for Helicoverpa armigera @ 4–5 per acre to monitor the population. Use light traps to attract and kill the adult moths. Biological Control: Apply, as needed, any one of the following: Azadirachtin 0.03% WSP (300 PPM) @ 1000 ml/acre. Bacillus thuringiensis var. kurstaki @ 200–250 ml/acre. Chemical Control: Emamectin benzoate 5 SG @ 80–90 g/acre in 200 liters of water, Spinosad 45 SC @ 50–64 ml/acre in 200 liters of water.

Question: How to control fruit and flower drops In Pomegranate?

Answer: To control flower and fruit drop in pomegranate under the Mrig Bahar system (June–July flowering for winter harvest), ensure timely irrigation without water stagnation, spray Borax at 0.1-0.2% (i.e., 1-2 grams per liter of water) to improve flower retention, apply NAA at 20–40 ppm (i.e., 1 ml of Planofix 4.5 SL in 4.5–5 liters of water) to reduce fruit drop, and control aphids by spraying Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 0.3 ml per liter of water during early infestation.

Question: How can I control fungal diseases in Coriander?

Answer: In coriander crop fungal diseases like powdery mildew, stem gall and seed-borne rots trouble farmers badly, plants become weak, leaves dry, seed setting goes down and finally yield and quality both suffer, especially when crop is late-sown and weather is humid with fog. To control this problem you must follow integrated management in simple step-by-step way. First is cultural control – always sow coriander timely between 30th October to 15th November to escape peak disease period, never sow again and again in same infested field, rotate with cereals or other non-host crops, keep proper spacing so sunlight and air circulation remain, and after harvest remove and destroy infected plant debris. For biological control – treat seed and soil with Trichoderma viride @ 2 kg per acre in 200 litres water, this suppresses fungi and improves root health, also use garlic clove extract spray or grow garlic and eucalyptus nearby as natural protectors. Do seed treatment – instead of only Carbendazim 3g/ kg of seeds, safer alternatives are Thiram 75 WP @ 500- 600g per kg seed, or Trichoderma viride @ 4 g per kg seed, even combination of GA3 (100 ppm) + Trichoderma 15 to 20 kg of coriander seeds in 10 to 15 litres of waters (2 ml per litre water). For chemical control use foliar spray for powdery mildew spray Propiconazole 25 EC @ 300 ml per acre in 400 litres water, or Hexaconazole 5 EC @ 400 ml per acre in 400 litres water, both sprayed twice at 15-day gap with PHI 14 days; for organic or low residue farming spray Wettable Sulphur 80 WP @ 2 kg per acre in 400 litres water, PHI 7 days; for stem gall, treat seed with Thiram 75 WP @ 3 g per kg and spray same @ 2 kg per acre in 400 litres water, PHI 7 days. Always do soil testing before sowing, balance fertilizers as per test, because healthy plants resist fungi better. And, very important is to rotate fungicides, never use same chemical repeatedly, spray in morning or evening for best effect, and always follow PHI strictly so that produce remains safe. If you can follow these combined method then coriander crop will stay healthy, diseases will remain under control, and finally yield and market price both will improve.

Question: what is the control of the curra murra disease (Leaf curl) of chilli?

Answer: "Curra Murra" is a local name for the devastating Chilli Leaf Curl Virus (ChiLCV), a viral disease that is a major problem for chilli farmers in Katni and other parts of Madhya Pradesh. The most prominent symptom is the upward curling, crinkling, and puckering of leaves. Infected plants show stunted growth with shortened internodes. Leaves are significantly smaller than normal and may appear brittle and leathery. Flowering is poor, and fruit formation is minimal or nonexistent. Any fruits that do develop are often small and deformed. Install yellow sticky traps at a rate of 4-6 traps per acre in your field to monitor and trap whiteflies. Plant two rows of maize, jowar, or bajra around the chilli field. Treat seeds with an insecticide like Thiamethoxam 70% WS @ 5 g/kg of seed before sowing. Drench the seedlings with Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 3.0 ml/10 liters of water for 30 minutes before transplanting. Apply Carbofuran 3G @ 4-5 Kg/acre in the mainfield.

Question: How can i get subsidy on paddy planter?

Answer: Farmers are eligible for government subsidies on the purchase of paddy transplanter machines to promote mechanized farming and reduce labor costs. Under this scheme, general category farmers can avail a 40% subsidy, while SC, ST, backward class, and women farmers are eligible for a higher subsidy of 50%. To apply, farmers must visit the e-Krishi Yantra Anudan Portal and submit required documents such as Aadhaar card, caste certificate (if applicable), B-1 land document, and a copy of their bank passbook. Additionally, a demand draft (DD) of ₹5,000 must be submitted to the district’s Assistant Agriculture Engineer as part of the application process. This subsidy helps make modern farming equipment more accessible, ultimately improving efficiency and productivity in paddy cultivation.

Question: What are the causes and management practices for leaf drying in Jamun in Sahibzada Ajit Singh Nagar region of Punjab?

Answer: Jamun is a summer–rainy season fruit crop, though the tree itself is perennial and remains green year-round. It is an evergreen fruit tree. Flowering: occurs in spring season (March–April). Fruiting/Harvesting: in summer to rainy season (June–July), sometimes extending till August depending on variety and region. symptoms small brown to dark spots appears on leaves (fungal leaf spot / blight). Margins of leaves turn yellow or brown, later become dry. Leaf tip or edges start scorching and curling. In case of dieback disease, the drying starts from leaf tip and twig ends, moving downward. If due to fungal disease (Anthracnose, Alternaria, Colletotrichum) → irregular necrotic patches, shot holes sometimes spray Copper Oxychloride (50 WP) → 500–600 g per acre in 200 L water, Mancozeb 75 WP (M-45) → 500 g per acre in 200 L water. If due to nutrient deficiency (esp. Zinc, Potash) → leaves become small, yellowed veins, later dry. If due to environmental stress → hot dry winds (loo), drought, or waterlogging cause general wilting and drying. for insect & pests (aphids, whitefly & caterpillar) - spray Dimethoate 30 EC → 400 ml per acre in 200 L water OR Malathion 50 EC → 400 ml per acre in 200 L water.

Question: What are some of the varieties of Bottle Gourd?

Answer: Bottle gourd is cultivated in Kharif and spring-summer seasons using improved varieties like PBOG-89 (GBPUAT, Pantnagar, 2010), which gives around 140 q/acre yield with a seed rate of 1.6-2 kg/acre.

Question: Information regarding the seed rate of Okra

Answer: For okra, use 4–5 kg of healthy, certified seed per acre for both summer and rainy seasons. Soak seeds in clean water for 6–8 hours before sowing to improve germination. Maintain row spacing of 45–60 cm and plant spacing of 15–30 cm for proper airflow and growth. Use resistant and high-yielding varieties like Hisar Unnat, Arka Anamika, or Parbhani Kranti, which are suitable for Haryana’s climate. You can buy certified seeds from local agri shops, FPOs, IFFCO, or authorized agri dealers such as the Haryana State Seed Certification Agency (HSSCA) or the Haryana Seeds Development Corporation (HSDC), to ensure better crop stand and pest tolerance. Avoid using old or damaged seed to prevent poor yield.

Question: How to control powdery mildew in the Ladyfinger crop?

Answer: Powdery mildew in Okra (Lady finger) is a common but severe disease caused by the fungus Erysiphe cichoracearum, which can significantly reduce plant vigour and crop yield. It appears as white flour-like powder on leaves and sometimes on fruits. It thrives in humid, cloudy weather. To manage this, use resistant varieties such as Arrka Anamika, Phule Utkarsha, maintain proper spacing for good air circulation in between, and avoid overhead irrigation. Or spray Neem oil 2% @20 ml/litre of water, or Wettable sulphur 80% @ 2-2.5 g/litre of water (800 g-1 kg per acre), or Hexaconazole 5% SC @ 1-2 ml/litre of water (200 ml per acre), or Tebuconazole 50%  + Trifloxystrobin 25% WG @ 0.5 g/litre (100 g per acre). Always spray in the morning or evening to avoid evaporation and better results. Rotate fungicides to prevent the development of resistance. Use appropriate safety gear such as a mask, gloves, goggles, full sleeve shirts, and boots. Always follow the PHI, that is, 7-10 days.

Question: What is the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme?

Answer: Farmers can access short-term crop loans and credit for allied agricultural activities through the central government's Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme, which provides loans up to ₹3 lakh at a interest rate of 7% per annum and loans up to ₹1.6 lakh under the KCC scheme are collateral-free, meaning the farmer does not need to mortgage their land or provide any other security to the bank.  Additionally the Government of Arunachal Pradesh has launched the Chief Minister’s Krishi Rinn Yojana, a state-level initiative providing an additional interest subvention of 4% reducing the effective interest rate to just 3% for eligible farmers. Moreover if the farmer repays the loan within one year an extra 3% rebate is given, it may be changes yearly. If you want to apply Kisan Credit card visit your nearest bank with land documents and ID proof.

Question: How to control ear caterpillars in Wheat?

Answer: Wheat is a rabi crop in India it is sown from October to November and harvested in March-April, It is not summer season crop. The ear caterpillar attacks wheat ear head  it is highly destructive pest it eats developing grains when they are in their milky or soft dough stage resulting in hallowed grains and significant yield loss. Question: How to control Cotton boll cracking?

Answer: Boll cracking is seen in cotton may be due to pest attack such as pink bollworm, which bores larvae into cotton bolls, irregular watering, or due to nutrient imbalances. The damage can cause premature ball opening or cracking and expose fibre and seeds to pests, diseases, and adverse weather, leading to reduced yield and fibre quality. To control this, sowing should be done at the recommended time(April to mid-May), apply a balanced fertilizer dose based on soil test recommendations, irrigate at critical stages, especially during flowering and ball development stage, avoid waterlogging situations, use Bt cotton and resistant varieties against bollworm, and remove and destroy infected cotton crop residue to reduce bollworm population.

Question: How can i do seed seed treatment in gram crop ?

Answer: No, chickpea (also known as gram) is not a major crop grown during the Zaid season in Madhya Pradesh. Chickpea is a major Rabi crop. The primary goal is to protect the seeds and young seedlings from key soil and seed-borne diseases such as wilt and dry root rot.  It helps protect the seedlings from early-stage insect pests. It promotes uniform germination and vigorous growth of seedlings. It facilitates better nutrient availability, particularly through bio-fertilizers. The recommended fungicides are Carbendazim (50% WP) at a dose of 2 grams per kg of seed or a combination of Carbendazim (1 g/kg of seed) + Thiram (2 g/kg of seed). The recommended bio-fertilizers are Rhizobium culture (for nitrogen fixation) and Phosphate Solubilizing Bacteria (PSB) or Phosphate Solubilizing Fungi (PSF) (for phosphorus availability). Use 100-200 grams of each culture per 10 kg of seed. Insecticide treatment protects the seedlings from pests like termites and cutworms during the early growth stage. Imidacloprid (70% WS) is a common systemic insecticide used for this purpose. The recommended dose is 3-5 grams per kg of seed. Apply the insecticide after the fungicide.

Question: How can I control White grub in Paddy crop?

Answer: White grubs are the larval stage of scarab beetles and are serious soil-dwelling pests of paddy. They feed on the roots of rice plants,causing reduced nutrient uptake, stunted growth, yellowing, and even plant death. Effective management requires an Integrated Pest Management approach combining cultural, biological, and chemical methods. Chemical control is most effective when targeted at the early larval stages,coinciding with pre-monsoon rains or soon after transplanting. Imidacloprid 17.8%WS is recommended at a dose of 10 -15 gm/kg seed. Chlorantraniliprole 18.5%SC is  effective option applied at 60-80 ml/acre as a soil drench. It provides long residual control and is generally safer for beneficial insects. Thiamethoxam 25%WG can be used at 80-100 grams/acre applied as a soil drench during peak adult activity. For a bio-rational approach, a combination of Metarhizium anisopliae fungus (2.5 kg) with a reduced rate of Imidacloprid (8 ml) mixed with FYM and broadcast per acre is highly effective. Always ensure the field has adequate soil moisture at the time of application for the insecticide to reach the root zone. Apply all chemicals during the evening hours to minimize degradation and target the pest when it is most active. Cultural controls like deep summer plowing to expose grubs and setting up light traps to catch adult beetles are crucial. Biological control using entomopathogenic fungi like Beauveria bassiana or nematodes provides sustainable management. Regular monitoring is essential; a threshold of 5-6 grubs/square meter is considered economically damaging.

Question: How can I control zinc deficiency in paddy crop?

Answer: The symptoms of zinc deficiency appear in paddy at 2-3 weeks after transplanting. The lower leaves become rusty brown near the base and ultimately dry up, yellow or white spot appear on older leaves,  while seedlings with zinc deficiency remain stunted and tillerless. To control this, apply 25 kg of zinc sulphate heptahydrate or 16 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate per acre to the soil at the time of last puddling before transplanting rice. In highly deteriorated soils, the symptoms of zinc deficiency sometimes appear in patches even after the application of the recommended dose of zinc sulphate. In that case, broadcast 10 kg of zinc sulphate heptahydrate or 6.5 kg zinc sulphate monohydrate per acre mixed with an equal quantity of dry soils on the affected patches. If deficiency symptoms appear during crop growth stage, foliar spray of 0.5% zinc sulphate solution(1 kg zinc sulphate heptahydrate per acre mixed with 500 gram unslaked lime in 100 litres of water) at weekly interval can help to correct the problem.

Question: give an information about SRI technology in Rice?

Answer: The System of Rice Intensification (SRI) is an innovative method of rice cultivation that helps improve productivity while using less water, seed, and fertilizer. In this method, very young seedlings (12-14days old) are transplanted with wider spacing of 25 × 20 cm, which promotes stronger plant and root growth. Irrigation is managed by alternate wetting and drying instead of continuous flooding, which saves about 30–40% water. Using a cono weeder regularly helps in controlling weeds and improving soil aeration and microbial activity. The use of organic manures like farmyard manure and compost instead of chemical fertilizers makes the method more environmentally friendly. Under proper management, SRI can increase yields to about 2.5–3.2 tonnes per acre, compared to 1.6–2 tonnes per acre in conventional methods, with better grain quality and lower pest incidence.

Question: What is the nursery sowing time of paddy in Faridabad?

Answer: The correct nursery sowing time for Kharif paddy depends on the specific variety you plant. For high-yielding non-Basmati (Parmal) types like PR 126 or PR 131, the ideal window for nursery sowing is from mid-May to the first week of June. For premium Basmati varieties like the world-famous Pusa Basmati 1121 or the early-maturing Pusa Basmati 1509, you must sow the nursery later, from the first week to the third week of June. This later sowing for Basmati is critical because it allows the crop to flower in cooler weather, which is the secret to getting its famous long grain and strong aroma that fetches the highest market price.
