Question: How to control basal rot in Onion?

Answer: Basal rot infected Onions show yellowing and dieback of the leaf tips at the early disease stage, which then progresses downwards. Below the soil, the roots rot, and the basal portion of the bulb becomes soft and watery. A whitish or pinkish fungal growth may be visible on the scales and roots of the bulb and the rot often continues to develop in storage, turning the bulbs into a soft, mushy mass. To control basal rot, an integrated approach combining cultural, biological and chemical measures is recommended. Practice crop rotation with non-host crops like cereals, avoid planting onions, garlic, or other Allium crops in the same field year after year, use disease-free planting material, remove and destroy infected plant debris to reduce the spread of the fungus, and ensure proper drainage to prevent waterlogging. Treat onion seeds with Carbendazim 50 WP at 2 grams per kg of seed or Thiram 75 WS at 2-3 grams per kg of seed. Drench soil around root zone with Carbendazim 50% WP @ 1 gram per litre of water at the appearance of early symptoms. If the symptoms persist, apply foliar spray of Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP @ 2.5 gram per litre of water, followed by second spray at 45 days using Tebuconazole 25% EC @ 1 gram per litre of water. Always rotate fungicide to prevent resistance and apply at 15 days interval for effective control. If you want to use biological option, treat seed with Trichoderma viride @ 6-10 gram per kg of seed before sowing, and apply Trichoderma viride 2.5 kg per acre in soil along with FYM before planting. In standing plants, you can drench soil with Trichoderma powder @ 10 g/litre of water near the stem region. For better control, dip the roots of the onion seedlings in a suspension of 10 grams of Trichoderma powder mixed with 100 grams of well-rotted FYM per litre of water for about 10 minutes.

Question: How should I treat Poplar cuttings before planting in Sangrur, Punjab?

Answer: The treatment of poplar cuttings is a crucial step in ensuring successful establishment and growth of the trees, especially in a region like Sangrur, Punjab, which is a major area for poplar agroforestry. Proper treatment helps prevent diseases and pests and promotes healthy root development. Rooting Hormones (Plant Growth Regulators) stimulate the development of a strong and healthy root system. IBA is a widely used and highly effective rooting hormone. To make your own solution, dissolve 10 mg of pure IBA powder in a small amount of  ethanol and then add water to make a final volume of 100 ml. Dip the basal (bottom) 2-3 cm of each cutting into the hormone solution just before planting. Fungicide treatment protect the cuttings from soil-borne fungal diseases that can cause rot and kill the young plant. The recommended dose for the fungicide Emisan 6 is 200 grams per 100 liters of water, while the insecticide Chlorpyrifos should be used at a dose of 250 ml per 100 liters of water. The cuttings should be submerged in this mixture for about 15-20 minutes. After this dip, and just before planting, the basal (bottom) end of each cutting should be treated with a rooting hormone to stimulate root development. This two-step process of chemical protection and hormone-induced rooting significantly increases the survival rate and ensures the healthy initial growth of the poplar trees.

Question: What is the seed treatment for Termites in Wheat?

Answer: Termites in Wheat attack roots and stems from below the soil, causing wilting and plant death in patches, especially in dry conditions. To control termites in wheat do seed treatment using 10 ml Thiamethoxam 30 FS or 1.2 ml Imidacloprid 600 FS as per kg of seed.

Question: How to CONTROL leaf-eating caterpillar ON Citrus?

Answer: Leaf Eating Caterpillar (LEC) is a common pest that affects orange orchards by feeding on young leaves, buds, and shoots, leading to defoliation and reduced fruit yield. To control LEC, cultural practices like pruning and destroying infected plant parts can help reduce the pest population. In biological control, release Trichogramma chilonis (egg parasitoids) at 50,000–100,000 per acre at weekly intervals during the egg-laying period. Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) at 400–500 g per acre (or 1–2 g per liter) during early larval stages In severe cases, chemical control can be adopted using Spinosad 45 SC at 1 ml/liter with waiting period 5 days, Emamectin Benzoate 5 SG at 0.5 grams/liter with waiting period 7 days, or Chlorantraniliprole 18.5 SC at 0.3 ml/liter with waiting period 10 days. Spraying should be done during early morning or late evening to minimize harm to beneficial insects and ensure better pest control.

Question: How should I prepare the field for sowing a new Kharif crop?

Answer: After harvesting the previous crop(Rabi crop), remove all plants stubble, debris and weeds. This is most important to prevent the carry over of pests and diseases to next crop. Use mouldboard plow or disc plow to break up compacted soil, improve aeration and water filtration in soil. If possible, conduct a soil test to determine the nutrient status and pH level of your field. This will help you decide the exact fertilizer and amendment requirements for the new crop.Apply well-decomposed Farm Yard Manure (FYM) or compost to the field. This is a crucial step as organic matter improves soil structure, water-holding capacity, and provides essential nutrients over time. It should be applied and mixed into the soil during the primary tillage. If you have time and resources, you can grow a green manure crop like sunnhemp or dhaincha in the pre-monsoon period. This crop is then incorporated back into the soil to improve fertility and soil properties.  Perform 1-2 rounds of shallow tillage using a cultivator or harrow. This breaks up the clods left from the primary tillage, create a fine and uniform seedbed. Ensure proper leveling of the field to avoid waterlogging and to ensure uniform irrigation.  Depending on the crop (e.g., maize, groundnut, cotton) and the irrigation method, you may need to form ridges and furrows or raised beds, this helps in efficient water management and drainage especially in a high rainfall environment. Apply basal dose of NPK fertilizers along with micronutrients as per soil test recommendations or crop wise local agricultural guidelines. The fertilizer should be broadcasted and mixed well into the soil before final harrowing.

Question: How to control broad leaf weeds in Wheat crop?

Answer: If broadleaf weeds are seen in wheat, spray 2,4-D Amine Salt 58% SL at 345 g per acre mixed in 200 litres of water. Apply this herbicide 20–30 days after sowing, when the wheat crop is at 3–4 leaf stage and weeds are still young for best control. Always spray on a clear, dry day with no wind or rain forecast. Use a fan-type flat nozzle for even coverage on the weed foliage. Avoid spraying during strong wind or rainy weather to prevent drift and poor result. Clean the sprayer properly before and after use. Early and timely spraying gives best weed control and ensures good crop growth. As a important note: Avoid spray drift to nearby crops like mustard or vegetables, as they are sensitive to 2,4-D.

Question: how to control aphid in coriander?

Answer: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that attack coriander crop. They make leaves curl, plants look weak, and release a sticky honeydew which brings black sooty mold, reducing seed and leaf yield badly. If not managed in time, bhai, they can spoil the whole crop. If want to manage it first keep the field clean, remove old residues, do crop rotation with cereals or pulses, and use mulching or intercrop with marigold to reduce landing of aphids, keep proper spacing (30 cm row to row, 10–15 cm plant to plant) so airflow is good. To protect natural friends like ladybird and lacewing which eat aphids. You can also use bio solutions like Lecanicillium 0.5–1 kg or Beauveria bassiana 1–2 kg in 200 litre water, no PHI, fully safe and works well in humid conditions. Also you can spray Neem-based Azadirachtin (10,000 ppm) – 200 ml per acre in 200 litres water, which is safe and eco-friendly or Trichogramma 1–2 lakh ( 100,000 to 200,000 parasitoids) per acre release is also good which controls eggs, used as biocontrol agent, released directly. If attack becomes high then go for chemical spray like Spinosad 75 ml or Imidacloprid 40-60 ml mixed in 200 litres water, sprayed when aphid population crosses economic threshold (~5 aphids/plant). As an alternatively you may use Thiamethoxam 25% WG @ 40 g per acre mixed in 200 litres water is another effective option. For safer option you may use Azadirachtin 10,000 ppm (Neem based) @ 200 ml per acre in 200 litres water for eco-friendly control, and spray in morning or evening when aphids are active and repeat sprays at 30-35 days interval or as per pest monitoring.. For extra safety, do seed treatment with Thiamethoxam 5 FS @ 5 g/kg seed with polymer coating and beneficial microbes like Azospirillum (120 g/kg seed) and Trichoderma viride (4 g/kg seed) provides early protection. Aftter chemical spray wait at least for Spinosad 45% SC and Azadirachtin 10,000 ppm (Neem based), Imidacloprid 17.8% SL 7days and for Thiamethoxam 25% WG keep15 days gap before harvest, don’t allow excess moisture in field, and apply balanced fertilizer as per soil test so that plants stay strong. If you follow this, aphid damage will remain very low and you will get healthy seed and fresh green leaves of coriander with good profit.

Question: How can I control Tur Pod bug in Arhar?

Answer: Pigeon pea (Arhar) is grown in the Kharif season in Madhya Pradesh because it needs warm weather and monsoon rains for good growth and flowering. In the Zaid season, there is high heat with very little rainfall, which does not support its growth. For managing the Tur pod bug (Clavigralla gibbosa), you should implement cultural practices like timely sowing of short-duration varieties, avoiding dense planting, and deep summer ploughing every 2–3 years to destroy pupae. In the field, install 20 bird perches per acre to attract predatory birds and utilize light traps (1 per 5 acres) to kill adult moths. Biological control involves applying a 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) spray during the flowering and pod formation stages or spray neem oil (10, 000 ppm) at a dose of 1 liter per acre. If the pest population exceeds the economic threshold (ETL), which is 10% affected pods, chemical intervention is necessary, with options including Flonicamid 50 WG at 80 g/acre (Pre-Harvest Interval : 7 days) or Acephate 75 SP at 200-240 g/acre (Pre-Harvest Interval: 7-14 days), sprayed by mixing in 150-200 litres of water for full plant coverage. Always rotate chemical insecticides from different groups to prevent resistance and, for best results, apply chemical sprays in the early instar stage of the pest.

Question: How to control Whitefly in Uradbean(Black gram)?

Answer: Whiteflies are present on the lower surface of the leaves and suck the juice, due to which the plants become weak and start drying. They transfer the virus to the plants through their saliva and spread a disease called Mungbean Yellow Mosaic Virus (MYMV). Yellow mosaic disease is very destructive, so it is essential to control whiteflies at an early stage. For effective control, an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) combining cultural, mechanical, biological, and chemical measures is recommended. Uproot and destroy the yellow mosaic disease-affected plants, choose black gram varieties that are tolerant or resistant to yellow mosaic virus (YMV) such as Pant U-30, install yellow sticky traps at 8-10 per acre to monitor and attract whitefly, and keep the field and surrounding area weed-free. Encourage natural predators like ladybird beetles, lacewings, and minute pirate bugs, spray biopesticides like Verticillium lecanii or Beauveria bassiana and neem seed kernel extract @ 5%. Chemical control should be used when the whitefly population reaches the economic threshold level (ETL), which is typically 5-10 adults per leaf or the yellow mosaic symptom. The recommended chemical insecticides for controlling whiteflies are: Imidacloprid 17.8 SL @ 60 ml per acre in 200 litres of water or Thiamethoxam 25 WG @ 40 grams per acre in 200 litres of water or Dimethoate 30 EC @ 200 ml per acre in 200 litres of water. Rotate insecticide to prevent resistance, always spray during early morning or late afternoon and maintain a PHI(Pre Harvest Interval) period of 21 days for these chemical.

Question: What is the proper way to apply Chloro 20 (1 litre) mixed with 10 kg during irrigation?

Answer: Chloro 20 (Chlorpyrifos 20% EC) is a banned pesticide for Ber, Citrus and Tobacco for its high level of toxicity. which is widely used for termite, soil insect, and sometimes cutworm control. The method and dose of application matter a lot for effectiveness and safety.

The proper way to apply Chloro 20 (Chlorpyrifos 20% EC) during irrigation is to take 1 litre of the formulation, mix it thoroughly with about 10–15 kg of clean sand or well-decomposed farmyard manure (FYM), and then apply this mixture directly into the irrigation channel so that it flows evenly with the water into the crop’s root zone. This method ensures uniform distribution of the chemical in the soil and provides effective protection against soil insects such as termites and cutworms. Care should be taken to use protective clothing while handling, avoid contaminating fish ponds and drinking water, and to observe the recommended pre harvest interval of 30 days.

Question: Guidance on plant growth in Bathinda region of Punjab?

Answer: Plant growth is the increase in size and development of a plant from germination to maturity, influenced by factors like sunlight, water, nutrients, temperature, and air quality. In Punjab, managing these factors at key growth stages is vital for crop success. For example, wheat requires irrigation around 20–25 days after sowing during the Crown Root Initiation stage to ensure strong root development and good tillering. Balanced fertilization, especially split application of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium based on soil testing, supports healthy growth. Using growth regulators like gibberellic acid and biostimulants such as seaweed extract can further enhance crop vigor. Timely weed control and pest management are essential to reduce competition and damage. Incorporating organic matter and amendments like gypsum improves soil fertility, especially in problematic soils.  managing growth through irrigation at critical growth stages for the main local crop, Wheat (e.g., the Crown Root Initiation stage), or using a specific plant growth regulator in a crop like Cotton. By following such integrated practices adapted to Punjab’s climate and soils, farmers can promote robust plant growth and improve yields.

Question: Is bloating a serious problem in cattle?

Answer: Bloating is a serious problem in animals like cows and buffaloes when too much gas builds up in the stomach, especially on the left side. There are two types of bloat. The first is free-gas bloat, where gas is trapped and can usually be removed using a stomach tube. The second is frothy bloat, where the gas forms bubbles and foam, and a tube does not help. In this case, an anti-foaming liquid, like a commercial drench or even vegetable oil, should be given to break the foam. Bloating is often caused by eating too much green grass, spoiled food, or eating too fast. The animal may look uncomfortable, stop eating, or have trouble breathing. As first aid, the farmer should make the animal stand, walk slowly, and gently massage the swollen left side while waiting for the vet. To prevent bloat, animals should be given a balanced diet of green and dry fodder and should not be overfed. Immediate care and correct treatment are very important to save the animal.

Question: How to control karnal smut in wheat?

Answer: To control Karnal Smut (Karnal smut) of wheat is a major seed-borne fungal disease that severely affects wheat grain quality and marketability. It is not a problem in kharif, because wheat is a Rabi season. Symptoms are Black powdery smut in few grains per spike, use crop rotation, use resistant varieties like WH1105, chemical control like Fungicide seed treatment Tebuconazole 2% DS @3 g per kg seed at before sowing can prevent the diseases. and use certified disease-free seed. quarantine-significant disease because it can have serious implications for international trade, seed movement, and crop productivity.

Question: How to establish a Farmer Producer Organization(FPO) group?

Answer: To form a Farmer Producer Organization (FPO) in Arunachal Pradesh, gather a group of minimum10-20 interested farmers, then register as a Producer Company under Section 465–581A of the Companies Act, 2013. Next, prepare all necessary documents, including identity proofs, residency certificates, landholding details, and a business plan, along with drafting bylaws or a memorandum of association. Submit the registration application and documents to the appropriate authority and open a bank account in the FPO’s name. After registration, approach the District Agricultural Office or relevant state agencies to apply for government support under the Central Sector Scheme for Formation and Promotion of 10,000 FPOs, submit proposals to avail financial assistance such as infrastructure funding, subsidies, equity grants, training, and market linkages. Finally, set up operations by establishing physical infrastructure, begin collective activities like input procurement, production, value addition, and marketing, and ensure compliance with governance, reporting, and audit requirements. Throughout the formation process, local Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) and the state agriculture department frequently offer direction and assistance.

Question: What soyabean varieties are good for Hoshangabad, Madhya Pradesh?

Answer: For the cultivation of soybean in Madhya Pradesh use varieties like J.S-335 with average yield of 10-12 quintals/acre, J.S. 93-05 with average yield of 8-10 quintals/acre, J.S. 95-60 with average yield of 8-10 quintals/acre, J.S. 97-52 with average yield of 10-12 quintals/acre, J.S. 20-29 with average yield of 10-12 quintals/acre, J.S. 20-34 with average yield of 8.8-10 quintals/acre, NRC-7 with average yield of 10-14 quintals/acre, NRC-12 with average yield of 10-12 quintals/acre or NRC-86 with average yield of 8-10 quintals/acre. For sowing, determine the quantity of seeds according to the size of the grains. For small grain varieties, use 24-28 kg of seeds per acre. For large grain varieties, determine the quantity of seeds at 32-36 kg per acre. During sowing, maintain a row spacing of 40 cm for less-spreading varieties such as JS-93-05 and JS-95-60, and 45 cm for more-spreading varieties like JS-335, NRC-7, and JS-97-52, which helps plants grow well, reduces competition, and ensures better yields.

Question: What is the recommended dose of fertilizers for Soybean in Madhya Pradesh?

Answer: Soybean is mainly grown in the Kharif season (June–October) because it needs warm weather (25–30°C), good soil moisture, and regular rainfall for germination and pod development. In the Zaid season (March–June), high temperatures and lack of sufficient water make conditions unsuitable for soybean growth and reduce yields. Apply 4-8 tons of well rotten Farm Yard Manure per acre at the time of last ploughing. Then apply 18 kg urea, 160-200 kg Single Super Phosphate (SSP) and 27 kg Muriate of Potash per acre before sowing. If the soil is deficient in Zinc, then apply 10 Kg Zinc Sulphate per acre at the time of sowing.

Question: How to control fruit dropping in Aonla (Indian Gooseberry)?

Answer: To control fruit dropping in Aonla (Gooseberry), it is important to understand the causes: Environmental stress - Nutrient deficiencies (Zinc, Calcium, Boron), Hormonal imbalances, Pest and disease pressure. Management / Control Measures- Foliar spray at fruit set stage: Zinc sulfate – 0.2–0.3%, Boric acid – 0.1%, Calcium nitrate – 2%, Gibberellic acid (GA₃) – 40 ppm. Follow-up spray: NAA (Naphthalene Acetic Acid) 20 ppm, 10 days later and These sprays improve pollination and fruit set, and hormonal sprays help prevent premature fruit drop, which has been shown to increase fruit retention and yield in Aonla.

Question: Give information regarding paddy (pr 123) variety in moga region ?

Answer: https://www.apnikheti.com/en/pn/agriculture/crops/cereals/rice#20MAY-5JUNE           PR 123 is an improved variety of Paddy .It is semi dwarf, stiff strewed variety with dark green and erect leaves. Its grains are long, slender and translucent. It is moderately resistant to bacterial blight pathogen. It gives average yield of 29 qtl/acre.PAU-recommended varieties such as PR 126, PR 131, or PR 121.

Question: How can I control purple blotch in Onion?

Answer: Purple blotch in onion, caused by the fungus Alternaria porri, is a serious disease in Ludhiana, Punjab, especially during humid or cloudy weather in the Rabi season. It appears as small, water-soaked lesions on leaves that turn purplish-brown with yellow margins, leading to drying of the leaf tips and reduced bulb size. Practice a rotation of 2-3 years or longer with non-host crops like small grains or corn to break the disease cycle and reduce pathogen buildup in the soil. Avoid dense plantings, as this can increase humidity and promote disease development. For chemical control, fungicides like Mancozeb 75% WP (600–800 g/acre), Propiconazole 25% EC (200 ml/acre), or Azoxystrobin + Tebuconazole (200 ml/acre) can be sprayed using 200 litres of water per acre. These should be applied at intervals of 10–14 days depending on disease pressure, and always with respect to the Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI), which is 7–14 days based on the chemical used. Rotating fungicides is important to prevent resistance development and ensure long-term effectiveness.

Question: Which improved varieties of wheat are suitable in CHHINDWARA region under MP district?

Answer: In Madhya Pradesh wheat farming gives best result only when you sow on right time with right variety, so remember sowing time is Rabi season from 15 October to 15 November, this window gives best yield and also saves crop from diseases, late sowing till November end is possible if irrigation is there but early sowing always gives better crop, for varieties government recommends Lok-1, HI-8663 (Poshan), HI-1531 (Harshita), GW-322, JW-3173, JW-3382, JW-3211, Sujata, C-306, Amar, Amrita, Malavshree, Malav Shakti, HD-4728, HI-8759 (Pusa Tejas), HI-8737 (Pusa Anmol) and among them Lok-1 and GW-322 are famous for high yield and drought tolerance, Sujata is sharbati wheat with high protein, and HI-8663 (Poshan) is special bio-fortified for good nutrition, seed rate should be 40 kg per acre with spacing of 22–23 cm row to row and for late sown wheat reduce the line spacing to 15-18 cm and depth of 4–6 cm, crop gets ready in 120–140 days around March-April, with good management and MP govt varieties you can easily get 18–22 quintal per acre, so just follow certified seed, timely sowing, proper spacing, soil test for balanced fertilizer and crop rotation with pulses and you will get healthy wheat crop and strong income for your family.

Question: How can I control flower drop in cotton crop?

Answer: Flower drop is a significant problem in cotton cultivation that can severely reduce yield. While a certain amount of flower dropping (around 30-40%) is a normal physiological process for the cotton plant to manage its fruit load, but excessive shedding needs to mange. Flower drops occur in cotton may be due to several reason such as lack of water or excessive water application, high temperatures, nutrient imbalance(especially Nitrogen, Boron and Calcium), and pest and disease incidence. To control flower dropping in cotton, maintain optimal soil moisture, avoid waterlogging conditions by providing proper drainage, and apply NPK fertilizer based on soil test results. For severe flower drop, spray Planofix(Naphthalene Acetic Acid ) 4.5 SL @ 5 ml per 10 litres of water before flowering stage and repeat after 15-20 days if needed, which is very effective for controlling flower drop in cotton. Pests and diseases can contribute to flower dropping in cotton crops. Monitor your crop regularly and implement integrated pest management (IPM) practices to minimize pest populations and also identify and manage diseases promptly to prevent flower drop.

Question: What is the SMAM scheme and how can I apply it?

Answer: The Sub-Mission on Agricultural Mechanization (SMAM) is a centrally sponsored scheme that promotes agricultural mechanization across India, including Arunachal Pradesh. It generally provides a 40% subsidy for individual farmers (50% for SC/ST, women). In the North Eastern region, including Arunachal Pradesh, subsidy rates can go up to 80–90% for certain equipment, and approved farmer groups or entrepreneurs can receive financial assistance of up to ₹10 lakh for setting up Custom Hiring Centres. If you want to apply, visit https://agrimachinery.nic.in and submit the required documents such as Aadhaar, land records, bank details, and ID proof. It is also recommended to visit your District Agriculture Office and check the Arunachal Pradesh state agriculture portal for the latest NE-specific higher subsidy rates and updated guidelines.

Question: Give information regarding RRTC?

Answer: The Regional Research and Training Centre (RRTC) in Tarn Taran is located at Booh village and is affiliated with Guru Angad Dev Veterinary and Animal Sciences University (GADVASU), Ludhiana. It is established to support farmers in the region, and focuses on training, research, and technology transfer related to veterinary and animal sciences, dairy, fisheries, and allied sectors. It also organizes various training programs, demonstrations, and welfare camps to benefit the local farming community. Farmer can directly visit the RRTC/KVK campus at Village Booh, Tarn Taran, where the Deputy Director or Programme Coordinator can be contacted for guidance and assistance.

Question: How to control insect pests in Beans?

Answer: Beans in Madhya Pradesh are highly susceptible to several insect pests that can cause significant damage. The most common and destructive insects are the borers, jassids, aphids, and whiteflies. An Integrated Pest Management (IPM) approach is the most effective way to control these pests, combining cultural and chemical methods. Remove and destroy any old crop debris and weeds from the field, as they can harbor pests and their eggs. Summer deep ploughing helps to expose and kill pupae of pests like the shoot and fruit borer in the soil. For monitoring and mass trapping of the shoot and fruit borer moths, install 4-5 pheromone traps per acre. Place 15-20 yellow sticky traps per acre to monitor and trap sucking pests like whiteflies and jassids. When the pest population reaches the economic threshold level, chemical intervention is necessary. For the Shoot and Fruit Borer, you can use Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC @ 60 ml per acre (PHI: 3 days), Flubendiamide 39.35% SC @ 60-70 ml per acre (PHI: 7 days), Emamectin Benzoate 5% SG @ 60-80 ml per acre (PHI: 3 days). For Sucking Pests (Whiteflies, Aphids, Jassids), you can use Imidacloprid 17.8% SL @ 40-50 ml per acre (PHI: 7 days), Acetamiprid 20% SP @ 40-60 grams per acre (PHI: 5-7 days), Spiromesifen 22.9% SC @ 250 ml per acre (PHI: 7 days). Use a high volume of water, typically 200-250 liters per acre, to ensure the spray reaches all parts of the plant, especially the underside of the leaves.  To prevent insecticide resistance, do not use the same chemical class repeatedly. Apply the spray in the early morning or late afternoon when temperatures are lower and the wind is calm.

Question: Can I get the contact number of the Director of Extension Education in Ferozepur, Punjab?

Answer: if you want direct and trusted advice for your farming problems, the best place is Punjab Agricultural University (PAU), Ludhiana. Here the Director of Extension Education office is fully for farmers like us. They guide on varieties, fertilizer doses, pesticides, seed treatment, crop rotation, water use, and everything which is PAU-approved and safe. You can call Director of Extension Education, at 0161-2401644 (office) or mail him at directorext@pau.edu. If needed, you can also reach Additional Director, at 94176-26843 or adee@pau.edu. Call them in office hours, they give practical, field-ready solutions directly suited for Punjab soils and crops.

Question: How to use Ziam in paddy?

Answer: In Punjab’s paddy (dhaan) fields,  Ziam is a ready-mix fungicide containing Hexaconazole 4% + Zineb 68% WP, and it works very well against stem rot caused by Sclerotium oryzae, plus it also helps control sheath blight and other fungal problems. The benefit is double — Hexaconazole stops the fungus inside the plant, and Zineb protects the plant surface so the disease doesn’t spread further. For stem rot, as soon as you see the first signs — black rotting at the stem base, white fungus growth, and mustard-like sclerotia — dissolve 300–400 g Ziam per acre in about 200 litres of water and spray with a knapsack or power sprayer, ensuring the spray is directed at the base of the tillers. Cover the plants evenly, but don’t spray in strong midday sun; early morning or late afternoon is best. If needed, repeat after 10–12 days, and always keep a 15-day PHI before harvesting for safe grain. In badly infected fields, drain out extra water for 4–5 days and avoid giving too much nitrogen, as stem rot loves wet, humid conditions. As an alternative, you can use other Punjab-approved fungicides like Hexaconazole 5% EC @ 400 ml/acre, Propiconazole 25% EC @ 200 ml/acre, or Validamycin 3% L @ 400 ml/acre in 200 litres water. For longer-term control, mix Trichoderma harzianum @ 1 kg/acre with FYM and apply at puddling or transplanting to cut down fungus in the soil. By using Ziam or its alternatives on time, along with resistant varieties like PR 126, PR 127, PR 128, proper water management, and removing old crop residue, you can keep stem rot under control, protect your yield, and get clean, good-quality grain for a better mandi rate.

Question: How should I treat Basmati rice nursery before transplanting?

Answer: Basmati paddy is a Kharif season crop, nursery is raised in June for transplanting in July. Nursery management plays a very important role in getting a healthy and uniform crop later. To grow healthy and uniform Basmati seedlings, it is very important to protect the nursery from diseases right from the start. For fungal diseases like blast and sheath blight, you can either drench the seedbed with a solution of Carbendazim 50 WP at 2 g per litre of water, or treat your seed with Trichoderma harzianum at 5 g per kg of seed before sowing. This will help prevent harmful fungi from attacking young plants. For bacterial blight prevention, mix Bleaching powder at 10 g per square metre of the nursery bed into the moist soil before sowing or dip the root of the seedlings in Streptocycline 0.02% solution for 30 minutes before transplanting. This reduces the risk of bacterial diseases. By following these steps, your seedlings will grow strong, disease-free, and ready for successful transplanting, helping you get a better quality and higher yield of Basmati rice.

Question: How to prepare urea in erode Tamil Nadu?

Answer: To prepare Urea Karaisal for the Kharif season in Erode, Tamil Nadu, dissolve 1 kg of urea in 100 liters of water to create a 1% urea solution. Apply this solution as a foliar spray at the early vegetative stage of crops like pulses, vegetables, or cereals. Use 10 g of urea per liter of water to ensure proper nitrogen uptake. Foliar sprays are most effective when applied in the early morning or late evening, avoiding the intense midday sun to prevent evaporation and minimize leaf burn. This method provides essential nitrogen to boost plant growth, enhancing leaf and root development, without the need for sugar or jaggery, which may promote microbial contamination.

Question: What are the best methods to control termite attack in Cotton crop?

Answer: In cotton during the zaid season, termites attack young plants by feeding on roots and stems near the soil surface, causing plants to wilt and die. Early signs include wilting seedlings and visible termite tunnels around roots. If infestation is noticed, apply imidacloprid 30.5% SC @ 2.1 ml/L around plant base or use fipronil 5% SC @ 1 ml/L as soil drenching, before sowing. Maintaining field hygiene by removing old crop residues and stubbles helps reduce termite habitats. Also, avoid excessive irrigation, as moist soil encourages termite activity. These measures together help protect cotton crops from termite damage effectively.

Question: Give information regarding kesar (saffron)?

Answer: Saffron (locally known as Kesar) is a very high-value spice crop, but unfortunately the climate of Punjab is not suitable for its successful cultivation. Saffron requires a cold and dry climate with warm summers and very cold winters, which is naturally found in areas like Kashmir and some hilly regions. In Punjab, the winters are not cold enough and summers are too humid, which leads to rotting of saffron corms and very low flower yield. If you are interested in saffron farming, it is better to consider contract farming or joint ventures in Jammu & Kashmir or Himachal Pradesh where the climate is suitable. For farmers in Punjab, experts recommend going for other high-value alternatives such as marigold, chrysanthemum for flowers, or aromatic crops like mentha, lemongrass, or stevia, which are well adapted to Punjab’s climate and also give good returns.

Question: How to control Fruit blast/Orange blast?

Answer: Citrus scab(Orange blast) affected fruits show water-soaked brown spots on the fruit's surface that turn into large black or brown spots and may drop prematurely. Orange blast is vulnerable during cool, wet, and windy conditions, so proper control measures should be adapted to reduce yield loss. To control and treat citrus scab (fruit blast) in orange, regularly prune out dead, infected twigs, collect and destroy infected fruits and plant debris, sanitize pruning tools between cuts to stop the spread, plant windbreak around the orchard field to protect it from strong winds, avoid the use of excessive nitrogen fertilizer in late season, ensure proper drainage to avoid waterlogging. Apply Copper Oxychloride 50 WP @ 600 grams in 200 litres of water or Bordeaux mixture 1% (1 kg copper sulphate+1 kg quick lime+100 litres water) immediately after fruit harvest and before the onset of the rainy season and repeat spray in April against in July, to August for effective control. The PHI(Pre-Harvest Interval) period for copper oxychloride and Bordeaux mixture is 7-14 days.

Question: What is the difference between MOP and SOP?

Answer: MOP (muriate of potash) and SOP (sulphate of potash) are highly demanded by farmers. MOP contains 60-61% K₂O (potassium oxide) 0-0-60 (0% nitrogen, 0% phosphorus, and 60% potassium) (10-20 kg/acre for fertigation for vegetables crops) and is preferred as a mid-range fertilizer, which is better for root development and fruit formation, reduces seedling damage, and is cheaper. MOP is mostly used in cereal crops like maize, wheat, groundnut, rice, etc., whereas SOP (0-0-50-46, with 0% nitrogen, 0% phosphorus, 50% potassium, and 46% sulfur) (15-25 kg/acre) is widely used for growing sensitive crops like fruits, vegetables, tobacco, etc. It is suitable for saline soils.

Question: Can you give me the information about Fisheries?

Answer: Fisheries in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh, are an important part of the local economy and food supply, driven by the district's various water bodies like dams, rivers, and ponds. The government's Department of Fisheries and various schemes aim to promote fish farming and support the local fishing community. Chhatarpur, like other parts of the Bundelkhand region, has a mix of dams, reservoirs, and ponds that are used for fish farming and fishing. The Rangwan Dam and Banisagar Dam are notable examples where a rich variety of fish species, both indigenous and cultured, are found. A study of the Rangwan Dam found a high fish diversity, with over 27 species. The fisheries in Chhatarpur and the broader region primarily focus on cultivating and catching commercially important fish. The main species include: Indian Major Carps (IMCs), Exotic Carps, and Catfishes. The Department of Fisheries in Madhya Pradesh implements several central and state-level schemes to develop the fisheries sector in districts like Chhatarpur. These schemes provide financial and technical support to fish farmers and fisher communities, such as Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (PMMSY), Mukhyamantri Machhua Samridhi Yojana, and National Agricultural Development Scheme (Rashtriya Krishi Vikas Yojana). The Department of Fisheries in Chhatarpur is responsible for implementing these schemes, providing training, and offering technical assistance to local fish farmers. For specific details on schemes or registration, farmers in Chhatarpur should contact the local fisheries office.

Question: Which improved varieties of Gram (Chana) are suitable for cultivation in Haryana?

Answer: Gram (chickpea) is a Rabi season crop and is not suitable for Kharif cultivation due to unfavourable climatic conditions such as high humidity and rainfall. Choose high-yielding varieties like HC-5, HC-1, and GNG-158. HC-5 and HC-1 varieties have been developed and released by Chaudhary Charan Singh Haryana Agricultural University (CCS HAU), Hisar, and are well suitable.GNG-158, developed in Rajasthan, but has excellent adaptability. these varieties give yield 10–12 quintals /ac under proper irrigated conditions.

Question: How much time does the effect of Coragen stays?

Answer: Coragen insecticide, containing Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC, is widely used for pest control in sugarcane crops.
It controls pests like shoot borers, top borers, stem borers, pyrilla, armyworms, etc. 
The protective effect of Coragen typically lasts for 10 to 14 days after application under normal field conditions. For proper dilution, use 1 to 1.5 ml of Coragen per liter of water when preparing the spray solution. The recommended application rate is 150 ml/acre, mixed in 200-250 liters of water for thorough coverage.
If pest pressure continues, a second application may be needed after 15 days, but limit to two applications per season.
The spray becomes rain-resistant approximately 2 hours after application, providing reliable protection. Coragen has a pre-harvest interval of 108-117 days, meaning no applications should be made within two weeks of harvest.

Question: What should be done if a cow does not drop the placenta after calving?

Answer: If a cow does not drop the placenta after calving,  it's a condition known as a retained placenta or retained fetal membranes. This is a common issue in cattle and requires specific management to prevent serious health problems. Do not manually remove the placenta, as this can lead to uterine damage and infection, trim excessive tissue hanging from the vulva if it causes contamination or distress, but do not attempt to pull or forcibly remove retained membranes and monitor the cow for signs of illness such as fever, loss of appetite, reduced milk yield, or abnormal discharge, massage the abdomen carefully to help release the placenta, walk the cow gently to stimulate uterine contractions and keep the cow in a clean and dry area to prevent infection. Ensure the cow receives adequate nutrition, especially Vitamin E and Selenium, which can help prevent and manage retained placenta, systemic antibiotics such as Penicillin or Oxytetracycline may be given if there are signs of uterine infection or systemic illness, consider giving a dose of oxytocin if the cow calved within the last 24 hours and is not experiencing contractions but this should only be done under veterinary guidance. Most cows will release the placenta naturally so avoid unnecessary intrauterine administrations or repeated antibiotics unless infection is present. If the cow shows any signs of illness, such as a high fever, foul-smelling discharge, or loss of appetite or does not expel the placenta within 24-48 hours, then immediately called a veterinarian .

Question: Information regarding mandi rate of Wheat crop

Question: How can I make Rose oil from Rose flowers?

Answer: Approximately 3,000 to 4,000 kg of fresh rose petals are required to produce 1 kg of pure rose oil. For small-scale production, a basic stainless-steel steam distillation unit (100–150 L capacity) suitable for small farmers or entrepreneurs can cost around ₹1.5–3 lakh, while larger commercial units may exceed ₹10 lakh. First you have to harvest fresh rose petals early in the morning → then separate petals from flowers → then gently crush or bruise them manually or mechanically to rupture cell walls (optionally mix with a little salt to aid rupture) → then load the crushed petals into a steam distillation or solvent extraction unit → then run the distillation/solvent process to release and collect oil vapours → then condense and separate oil from water or solvent → then purify the oil by filtration or vacuum distillation → and finally store the pure rose oil in airtight, dark glass bottles. Recommended rose types used to extract high-quality rose oil are: Rosa damascena (Pink Damask Rose), Rosa centifolia, Rosa rugosa, Rosa alba, and Rosa bourboniana.

For keeping your orchard weed-free you can go for two types of spray – pre-emergence and post-emergence; in pre-emergence, just after first showers of June, spray Diuron 1.2 kg per acre or Simazine 1.62 kg per acre, mixed in 200-250 littres of water and repeat again after 120 days around September. this will keep the garden clean almost 10 months; in post-emergence, when weeds already come, spray Glyphosate 1.62 liters per acre or Paraquat 0.81 liter per acre mixed in 200-250 liters of water per acre, but spray carefully before flowering and never let the chemical touch the main orange plants, this way weeds are fully controlled, trees grow healthy, and fruits come big and good in quality. Stop irrigation 1–2 months before flowering to improve flowering and fruit set, if flowering is poor spray CCC 1500–2000 ppm or paclobutrazol, prune unwanted branches to keep a healthy canopy, mulch the base with 8 cm layer of dry leaves or paddy husk to save moisture and improve fruit size, in young orchards take intercrops like pulses to use space and earn extra, and if you follow these steps properly you will get bigger fruit size, better yield.

Question: What causes bunchy top disease in banana plants?

Answer: Bunchy Top in banana is a viral disease spread by aphids, causing leaves to bunch up and plants to become stunted, reducing yield. To manage this problem, first use only healthy, disease-free planting material from trusted sources. Remove and destroy any infected plants immediately to stop the virus from spreading. Uproot Heliconia and destroy ant nests to reduce aphid reservoirs. To control the aphids, use Neem oil 3000 ppm (400-600 ml/acre) and if the infestation is severe then spray insecticides like Imidacloprid 17.8 SL at 40-60 ml per acre or Thiamethoxam 25 WG at 40 grams per acre, mixed in 200 liters of water. Maintain good field hygiene by keeping the orchard clean and removing weeds. Crop rotation and proper spacing also help reduce disease spread. Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI): Imidacloprid and Thiamethoxam have a PHI of 7 days. Please wait this time after spraying before harvesting.

Question: How can I protect my wheat crop from Karnal bunt disease in Ferozepur, Punjab?

Answer: In Wheat, Karnal bunt symptoms appear as few grains of ear is infected and partially filled with black powdery spores and often produce fishy odour. To control this, use karnal bunt resistance variety such as PBW 343, PBW 502, WHD 943, PDW 291, practice crop rotation withy non host crops such as maize, pulses, and collect, destroy bunt infected grains. Treat seed before sowing with Carboxin 37.5% + Thiram 37.5% DS @ 2 gram per kg or Carboxin 75% WP @ 2 gram per kg, and apply single spray of Propiconazole 25% EC @ 200 ml per acre in 200 litres of water at ear emergence stage. A PHI(Pre Harvest Interval) period of 30 days should be followed for Propiconazole on wheat if it is apply to control karnal bunt disease.

Question: What is the average yield of PAC-401 Hyola?

Answer: PAC 401 Hyola is a high-yielding hybrid rapeseed-mustard. The recommended seed rate for this variety is 1.5 to 2.0 kg/acre when using standard drilling methods. For line sowing, the lower end of this range (1.5 kg/acre) is typically sufficient, while broadcast sowing may require up to 2 kg/acre to ensure proper plant density. The average yield is up to (7.2 to 8.8 q/acre) under normal conditions. With improved agronomic practices yields upto (5-6q/acre) in some cases. For best results, you should use certified seeds from authorized dealers to ensure genetic purity and good germination rates. The variety shows moderate resistance to major diseases like white rust and alternaria blight, contributing to its yield stability

Question: How to control Aphids in Peas?

Answer: If the attack is low, that is below 20-25 aphids per plant, then it is best to install yellow sticky traps in the field at a rate of 4-5 for an acre. If the attack continues, make sure to use a powerful water spray to remove the aphids from the stem. 

As part od Biological control release 1st instar larvae of green lacewing (Chrysoperla zastrowsillemi) @ 4000/acre.

The next step is if the attack is continuing, then use neem oil 600 ml with 150 ml of soap in 150 Liters of water. This step has to be repeated in 7-10 days. If the attack continues, a chemical insecticide is needed, and it is usually Thiamethoxam 25% WG 80 grams mixed in 200 liters of water and spread evenly in the plant.
There has to be a waiting period of 7-14 days after applying the insecticide to avoid residue contamination of the produce.

Question: How to control Aphids in Chilli?

Answer: Aphids (Aphis gossypii) are a major threat to chilli crops during the Kharif season, especially under warm, dry conditions and high nitrogen levels. To control this pest, follow Integrated Pest Management (IPM) practices such as using resistant varieties, installing traps, and practicing crop rotation. Avoid continuous chilli cropping in the same field; intercrop with onion or garlic; and use biological control methods such as releasing ladybird beetles, green lacewings, and parasitic wasps @ 2,000 per acre to reduce aphid populations. Chemical control: Thiamethoxam 12.6% + Lambda-cyhalothrin 9.5% ZC: Apply 50–80 ml per acre; PHI: 3 days. Fipronil 5% SC: Apply 320–400 ml per acre; PHI: 7 days. Economic threshold: Apply control measures when 5–10 aphids per plant are observed.

Question: How can I control Alternaria Blight in Radish?

Answer: Alternaria blight in Radish is a fungal disease that causes small dark brown to black spots on the leaves. Slowly, the leaf edges dry up, and the plant becomes weak and stunted, which reduces growth and yield. The disease spreads more during cool and moist weather and also from infected plant waste if not removed from the field. To control it, spray Mancozeb 75% WP at 600–800 g per acre in 200 litres of water at the first appearance of symptoms. This helps stop the fungus from spreading. For better and longer protection, you can also spray a mix of Azoxystrobin 11% + Tebuconazole 18.3% SC at 300 ml per acre in 200 litres of water. If the weather stays moist, repeat the spray after 10–12 days if needed. Start spraying as soon as spots appear on leaves. Avoid overhead watering like sprinklers, as wet leaves increase the disease. Keep the field clean, avoid continuous radish cropping in the same land, use certified disease-free seeds, and practice 2–3 years crop rotation for better disease management. Remove old infected plants after harvest. By following these steps, you can protect your crop and improve your yield. All sprays mentioned are safe and commonly used in radish fields.

Question: Where can I get Paddy Transplanter?

Answer: Paddy transplanters are available for purchase through authorized agricultural machinery dealers located across major farming districts in Madhya Pradesh. These dealers represent well-known brands such as VST Tillers, Kubota, Mahindra, John Deere, and Yanmar. Alternatively, farmers can procure these machines through the MP State Agro Industries Development Corporation Ltd. or by applying via official government schemes designed to promote agricultural mechanization. A significant subsidy is available for purchasing a paddy transplanter under the Central Sector Scheme for the promotion of agricultural mechanization. The subsidy rate is set at fifty percent of the machine's cost. This financial support is subject to a ceiling limit of one point two five lakh rupees for a standard four-row paddy transplanter. The subsidy scheme is available to individual farmers, Custom Hiring Centers, and Farmer Producer Organizations. The price of a paddy transplanter varies considerably based on its type and features. A basic manual walk-behind model typically ranges from one point five to two point five lakh rupees. A more advanced four-row riding type transplanter can cost between three point 500000 to 650000 rupees. After applying the maximum subsidy, the effective out-of-pocket cost for a four-row machine would be approximately two point seven five lakh rupees for a model priced at four lakh rupees. The area a transplanter can cover depends on its type. A manual walk-behind transplanter operated by a single person can cover approximately zero point three to zero point four acres in a full day. A four-row riding type machine is significantly more efficient, capable of transplanting two to three acres per day during an eight to ten hour operating period. The application process for the subsidy is conducted online through the official MP State Agro Portal. Farmers must first register on the portal using their personal and land details. After registration, they can log in, locate the agricultural mechanization subsidy section, and select the paddy transplanter from the list of available implements. The application requires uploading necessary documents for verification by district agricultural officers. Once approved, the subsidy amount is transferred directly to the farmer's registered bank account.

Question: How can I manage prolonged heat in cattle?

Answer: In Punjab summer the long heat wave is very tough on our animals, it cuts milk, eggs and even makes buffalo, cow, goat or poultry weak. PAU experts say simple desi plus modern steps can save your animals and income. First of all, never leave them in open sun in the peak hours (12–4 pm), always keep shade or shed ready and give fresh cool water 3–4 times daily. Morning and evening give green fodder like berseem, maize or chaffed paddy straw, and if possible put fan, cooler or mist sprayer in the shed. Whitewash on walls and roof or thatch cover on poultry and goat house keeps inside temperature down, and one or two times cool water shower or spray makes animals feel fresh. For health side always add mineral mixture or electrolyte, about 50 gram per adult animal per day, in feed so body salts don’t drop. In dairy cows or buffalo, give yeast and buffer supplements as per packet to maintain digestion and milk fat. If animal shows panting or drooling, just shower with clean water, don’t panic. No medicine or injection needed, just shade, water and feed balance is the real cure. For mating, avoid the hot mid-day, best is early morning or evening service. Grazing also shift to cool hours. Always keep floor dry and bedding clean, otherwise foot rot and flies will come. And remember, if you ever use any spray or chemical, always strictly follow the specific withdrawal period mentioned on any chemical or drug’s label or as prescribed by your veterinarian before milk sale or slaughter. These small steps give us good milk, healthy goats and safe poultry even in Punjab’s loo winds.

Question: Can we use cow urine for spraying in berseem crop?

Answer: You can safely use cow urine spray on barseem because it acts as bio-fertilizer(supply N, K and other micronutrients) and bio-pesticides helps in reducing aphids, jassids, especially when it is fermented for 7-10 days and mixed with neem extracts and trichoderma. It is eco-friendly and residue free which is best for livestock crop like barseem and also improve soil microbial activity. It is recommended not to spray fresh undiluted cow urine directly on leaves as it can harm leaves, take 1 part of cow urine with 10 part of water and spray 80-100 litre diluted solution per acre using a knapsack sprayer at a interval of 20-25 days if needed. But always remember it is a supplementary input only, not as direct substitute of recommended fertilizers, fungicides and pesticides.

Question: How can we increase rice production in Betul district, Madhya Pradesh?

Answer: Betul district, located on the Satpura plateau, is a significant rice-producing region in Madhya Pradesh, with a climate and soil profile that are well-suited for the crop. To increase rice production, select high-yielding and region-specific varieties such as IR-64, MTU-1010, JRH-5, and hybrid varieties recommended by local agriculture universities. Prepare field with fine tilth, proper leveling, and bunding to ensure uniform water distribution. Employ alternate wetting and drying or System of Rice Intensification (SRI) methods to save water and improve root growth. In water stress areas, choose DSR method instead of traditional transplanting. It saves labor, reduces water requirements, and can be more cost-effective. Follow soil test-based nutrient management to apply optimal quantities of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrients like zinc and iron. Integrated nutrient management combining organic manures and chemical fertilizers improves soil health and productivity. Use healthy seedlings of optimum age (20-25 days) for transplantation or direct-seeding methods with appropriate spacing (20x15 cm) for better tillering and canopy development.  Monitor pest populations such as stem borers, leaf folders, and diseases like blast and bacterial blight. Implement integrated pest management with biological controls and judicious insecticide use. Timely application of herbicides like Pretilachlor or Pendimethalin in early crop stages, combined with manual weeding or mechanical weeders, reduces yield losses caused by weeds.

Question: What are the symptoms and control measures of caterpillar infestation in cashew?

Answer: Caterpillar attack in cashew young leaves , flower bunches and fruits. It is caused by Hairy caterpillar .
During the early stages when the caterpillar population is below economic threshold level that is just one caterpillar in a branch it is better to remove the caterpillar rather than spraying a chemical. 
If the population increases , spraying of insecticide like Lambda-cyhalothrin 5% EC at 120-150 ml per acre mixed in 200 liters of water or Emamectin Benzoate 5% SG at 80-100 grams per acre in 200 liters of water should be used. Rotate the chemicals to avoid resistance build up. Repeat the process in 7-14 days based on severity . Make sure to follow a waiting period of 5-7 days for both insecticides to avoid contamination.

Question: What is the reason for low milk production in my buffaloes?

Answer: Low milk yield in buffaloes is a common issue caused by a combination of factors such as poor nutrition, improper management, health disorders, and low genetic potential. Nutritional deficiencies, especially in protein, energy, and minerals, directly affect milk production. Inadequate supply of clean drinking water also limits yield. Health problems like mastitis, internal parasites, or reproductive issues further contribute to reduced milk output. Stress from poor housing, extreme temperatures, and irregular milking practices can also negatively impact lactation. To improve milk yield, buffaloes should be given a balanced diet including green fodder, dry roughage, concentrate feed, and mineral mixture. Clean water should be available at all times, and milking should be done regularly with proper hygiene. Housing must be clean, ventilated, and comfortable to reduce stress. Regular deworming, vaccination, and treatment of diseases are essential for animal health. Lastly, selecting high-yielding breeds or using artificial insemination with proven bulls can enhance milk productivity in the long term

Question: How can I control the cotton caterpillar?

Answer: Cotton crops are affected by several caterpillar pests, including the American bollworm, pink bollworm, spotted bollworm, and armyworm. An integrated pest management approach is the most effective strategy for control. Begin with cultural and mechanical practices. Use pheromone traps, placing 4 to 5 traps/acre for each pest species to monitor and trap adult moths. Practice deep summer plowing to expose and destroy pupae in the soil. Grow trap crops like marigold or okra around the field to attract pests away from the cotton. Handpick and destroy egg masses and larvae when spotted during regular field scouting. For biological control, conserve natural enemies like spiders and parasitic wasps. Release the egg parasitoid Trichogramma chilonis at 50,000 eggs/acre, making multiple releases at weekly intervals. Apply biopesticides like HaNPV at 100 larval equivalents/acre. Chemical insecticides should be used only when the pest population crosses the economic threshold level. Always rotate chemicals from different groups to prevent resistance. You should choose Chlorantraniliprole 18.5%SC should be applied at 60 to 70 ml/acre with an application interval of 12 to 15 days. Emamectin Benzoate 5%SG should be applied at 80 to 100 gm/acre with an application interval of 12 to 15 days. Spinosad 45%SC should be applied at 50 to 60 ml/acre with an application interval of 10 to 12 days. Indoxacarb 14.5%SC should be applied at 150 to 200 ml/acre with an application interval of 12 to 15 days. For best results, spray during the evening hours and ensure thorough coverage of squares, flowers, and bolls. Always wear appropriate protective gear when handling and applying chemicals.

Question: How to control Fruit borer in Brinjal Crop?

Answer: For effective management of shoot and fruit borer in brinjal, Intercropping of brinjal (2 rows) with
coriander (one row) or fennel (1 row) should be followed. Install pheromone traps @ 4-5/acre for
monitoring and 10/acre for mass
t rapping at 10 m distance from 20 DAT, the pheromone septa should be changed at regular interval. Place the traps either at canopy level or at slightly above the canopy level for effective attraction.

As part of Biological Control Release Trichogramma chilonis at
 20,000/acre/week commencing from 21 days after transplanting (based on adult activity) till end of the crop. Trichocards should be tied to sticks placed at 4-5 m apart in the field in the evening prior to 1 day of parasitoid
adult emergence. Conserve predators such as lady bird beetle, Seven spotted ladybird beetle,
Lacewing. Spray azadirachtin 1% EC (10000
 ppm) neem based EC @ 400-600 ml in 400 l of water/acre or azadirachtin 0.03% (300 ppm) neem oil based WSP @ 1000-2000 ml in 400-600 l of
water/acre.

For chemical control  lambda cyhalothrin 4.9% CS @ 200 ml in 200 l of water/acre or lambda cyhalothrin 5% EC @ 120 ml in 160- 240 l of water/acre. As an alternative Spinosad 45% SC @ 73 ml/acre ( in 200 liters of water) can be used. A pre- harvest interval of 5 days is needed in case of  lambda cyhalothrin and 3-5 days is needed for Spinosad to avoid contamination.

Question: What is NSFM & what are its uses?

Answer: Fisheries become the life-changing decision for many farmers, as they are getting large amounts of profit. If you want to build up your career in fisheries, you can go with the government scheme that is (Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana PMMSY) to promote sustainable fisheries, aquaculture, and marine development, its main aim is to enhance fish production, improve livelihoods, modernize infrastructure, and ensure sustainability. In aquaculture development you can get a 40-50% subsidy if you have a general category; if you have an SC/ST category, you can get a 60% subsidy. You have to collect all the necessary/beneficial information from District Fisheries Development Officer then you can apply for the NSFM scheme, you can apply from https://pmmsy.dof.gov.in. On this website, you verify your eligibility; after that, you have to submit the necessary documents, and then your application is reviewed by the District Fisheries Officer. After confirmation, the subsidy will be released in 2-3 installments. You can also apply at the State Fisheries Department or NCDC (National Cooperative Development Corporation).
